91.title: Meet Colonel Hunny Bakshi: Army Intelligence Officer Who Played Neem Karoli Baba in ‘Hanuman Ansh’
91.description: Colonel Munishwar Nath Bakshi, popularly known as Colonel Hunny Bakshi, is a retired Indian Army Intelligence Corps officer who once commanded the secretive
91.text:
Colonel Munishwar Nath Bakshi, popularly known as Colonel Hunny Bakshi, is a retired Indian Army Intelligence Corps officer who once commanded the secretive Technical Support Division (TSD). Years after a career associated with military intelligence and covert operations, the veteran officer took on a very different role — portraying Neem Karoli Baba, also known as Maharaj Ji, in the 2026 film Hanuman Ansh.

A recipient of the Vishisht Seva Medal (VSM), Colonel Bakshi was commissioned into the Military Intelligence Corps in December 1988 after training at the Indian Military Academy, Dehradun. His military career included assignments connected with Jammu and Kashmir, the Northeast and military intelligence operations.

Before taking charge of the TSD, he commanded a Military Intelligence unit in Kolkata between 2007 and 2010. He has spoken publicly about his operational experience, including involvement in counter-IED work and ceasefire-related assignments in the Northeast, and has said that he survived three IED attacks during his service.

Commanding the Technical Support Division

Colonel Bakshi became widely known because of his association with the Technical Support Division, an ad hoc Military Intelligence unit created in 2010 during the tenure of then Chief of Army Staff General V.K. Singh.

Bakshi was selected to raise and command the unit. Operating from Delhi Cantonment, the TSD was tasked with sensitive intelligence-related activities, with its work largely remaining outside the public domain.

Over the years, numerous claims about the unit’s activities have appeared in media reports and interviews. Bakshi himself has subsequently discussed aspects of the TSD and his intelligence career in public interviews. However, many operational details remain classified and several specific claims concerning its missions have not been independently confirmed through official records.

The TSD was disbanded in 2012 following General V.K. Singh’s retirement.

Years of Inquiries and Legal Proceedings

Following the closure of the TSD, Colonel Bakshi faced a turbulent period in his Army career. Several inquiries were initiated amid allegations concerning the functioning of the unit, including questions surrounding surveillance equipment, classified material and expenditure from secret funds.

He was eventually attached for General Court Martial proceedings. The proceedings were dropped in March 2018 after the court accepted a plea in bar concerning procedural and legal issues, including questions related to the Court of Inquiry and documents sought for his defence. No conviction resulted from the proceedings.

Bakshi later continued serving in the Army before taking premature retirement on November 5, 2019.

From Military Intelligence to Public Commentary

Following retirement, Colonel Bakshi emerged as a commentator on defence and national-security issues.

He has appeared in interviews and public discussions covering subjects including military intelligence, Kashmir, internal security, the Agnipath recruitment system, Khalistan-related security concerns and the situation in Manipur.

His experience with the Technical Support Division has also remained a major subject of public interest, particularly following his detailed interviews about the controversial intelligence unit.

Colonel Hunny Bakshi as Neem Karoli Baba

In an unexpected transition from military intelligence to cinema, Colonel Bakshi appeared as Neem Karoli Baba in the 2026 film Hanuman Ansh.

According to Bakshi’s account, his involvement with the project began after he approached director Vishal Chaturvedi with a script of his own. His physical resemblance to Neem Karoli Baba eventually led to him being offered the role of the revered spiritual figure.

The appearance marked an unusual new chapter for an officer whose professional life had previously revolved around military intelligence and national-security assignments.

From graduating from the Indian Military Academy and serving in the Intelligence Corps to commanding one of the Indian Army’s most discussed intelligence units, and eventually portraying Neem Karoli Baba on screen, Colonel Hunny Bakshi’s journey has taken him through remarkably different worlds.

93.text:
Around 4,000 people participated in the CCPUR Half Marathon 2026 in Churachandpur, Manipur organised by the 58 Battalion of the Central Reserve Police Force (CRPF) in collaboration with the Sports Authority of India (SAI), with a focus on promoting peace, harmony, fitness and a drug-free lifestyle among the youth.

The event aimed to encourage sportsmanship, healthy living and greater community participation, while providing young people with opportunities to engage in physical and sporting activities.

Churachandpur Deputy Commissioner Krishna Kumar appreciated the initiative taken by the CRPF and urged young people to promote peace and unity and stay away from drugs.

“My appreciation goes to the entire team of the CRPF battalion for taking such an initiative. To the youth, I would like to say: be a beacon of good hope, believe in peace and unity, and stay away from drugs,” Kumar said.

Commandant of the 58 Battalion CRPF, Suraj Phogat, said the marathon was organised to convey a message of peace and harmony in the area and provide young people with avenues to engage in sports.

He said sporting activities can help keep the youth engaged and prevent them from being diverted towards unhealthy or harmful activities.

“We believe that people out here are more interested in sports activities. Unless you engage the youth in such physical activities, they get diverted,” Phogat said.

Phogat said the participation of around 4,000 people was encouraging and expressed hope that future editions of the event would attract more than 10,000 participants.

He also said the CRPF plans to organise other sporting activities in the area, including football and volleyball, as part of its efforts to expand community engagement through sports.

94.title: ‘Very happy and proud of myself’: Mirabai Chanu after historic Asian Games silver
94.description: Mirabai Chanu won her first Asian Games medal with silver in the women's 49kg event. The result ended years of waiting and placed her in a rare group of Indian weightlifters.
94.text:
Indian weightlifter Mirabai Chanu said winning her first Asian Games medal was a moment she had waited years for, describing her silver in the women’s 49kg category at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games on September 23 as a source of immense pride.

The Tokyo Olympic silver medallist finished with a combined lift of 198kg to secure the silver medal. North Korea’s Ri Song Gum took gold with 215kg, while Wijayana finished with bronze.

“I am very happy. I have been waiting for this day for many years. Finally, I have won a silver medal. I am very happy and proud of myself. My dream has come true,” Chanu said after the event.

The 32-year-old said the Asian Games had been a major target for her, particularly after a demanding competition schedule. She acknowledged the pressure of competing at the continental event but said she had prepared with the specific goal of returning with a medal.

“There was a lot of pressure. The Asian Games are very important for me. It is very difficult for us to play back-to-back competitions. After the Commonwealth Games, I had only one month. This is what I wanted to do. I wanted to win at least one medal in the Asian Games. I prepared very well and won this medal,” she said.

Chanu completed all three of her snatch attempts, lifting 83kg, 85kg and 87kg. She then successfully lifted 107kg and 111kg in her first two clean and jerk attempts to finish with a total of 198kg.

The medal also marked redemption of sorts after her fourth-place finish at the 2023 Asian Games in Hangzhou. An injury forced her to withdraw from her final clean and jerk attempt, ending her hopes of a podium finish.

Chanu entered the Aichi-Nagoya Games on the back of a gold medal at the 2026 Commonwealth Games in Glasgow. She is a three-time Commonwealth Games champion and won Olympic silver at Tokyo 2020.

Her maiden Asian Games medal also places her in an elite group of Indian weightlifters. She became only the second Indian after Karnam Malleshwari to win medals at the Olympics, Asian Games, Commonwealth Games, World Championships, Asian Championships and Commonwealth Championships.

For Chanu, however, the immediate focus was simply on savouring a moment she had spent years chasing.

“I don't know where to start. I have been waiting for this day for many years. I am very happy and proud of myself. I want to celebrate this day,” she said.

Born in Nongpok Kakching, Manipur, Chanu began formal weightlifting training in 2008 and went on to become one of India’s most prominent weightlifters.

96.title: 7 high-risk glacial lakes identified in Arunachal’s Tawang, GLOF threat to villages
96.description: At least seven high-risk glacial lakes have been identified in the Mago area of Arunachal Pradeshâs Tawang district, posing a significant Glacial Lake Outburst Flood (GLOF) threat to downstream communities.
96.text:
Referring to recent devastating floods in the Himalayan region, officials urged residents of vulnerable areas to remain prepared

(With agency inputs)





TAWANG: At least seven high-risk glacial lakes have been identified in the Mago area of Arunachal Pradeshâs Tawang district, posing a significant Glacial Lake Outburst Flood (GLOF) threat to downstream communities.The Arunachal Pradesh State Disaster Management Authority (APSDMA), in collaboration with the District Disaster Management Authority (DDMA), Tawang, and the State Disaster Response Force (SDRF), has launched an extensive awareness and training programme on GLOF risks for communities living downstream of the high-risk glacial lakes in the Mago area under Thingbu Circle.The awareness campaign commenced at Mago village, with a special focus on vulnerable downstream habitations, including Duri village, as well as the Indian Army camp situated in the area.According to news agency ANI, residents were briefed on the location, altitude and distance of the identified high-risk glacial lakes from their settlements, as well as the potential threats posed by a sudden glacial lake outburst.Senior Consultant Dr Bhupen Mili explained the causes and mechanisms of GLOFs, their possible impact on downstream settlements, and the estimated time floodwaters could take to reach Duri village, the Army camp and other vulnerable locations following such an event.Participants were sensitised to the importance of identifying safe evacuation routes and designated locations, following proper evacuation procedures, and preparing effective community-level plans to minimise risks to lives and property.Deputy director, SDMA, Dorjee Khandu said seven high-risk glacial lakes have been identified in the Mago area, six of which share a common downstream drainage system passing through several villages, including Duri.He stressed the need to establish locally suitable and effective early-warning mechanisms so that alerts can reach every resident in time. He also emphasised prompt dissemination of warnings to downstream settlements in the event of a GLOF, particularly as Duri village would be among the first settlements likely to experience the impact of floodwaters.Referring to recent devastating floods in the Himalayan region, Khandu urged residents of vulnerable areas to remain prepared and, where necessary, gradually move to safer locations.He said that although natural disasters of such magnitude cannot always be prevented, preparedness, effective early warning and timely evacuation can significantly reduce risks to lives and property.DDMO, Tawang, Gendan Tsomu, urged villagers to participate sincerely in the training and make the most of the life-saving techniques being taught by resource persons.She also appealed to participants to share the knowledge and skills gained during the programme with their families, friends and the wider community to ensure preparedness reaches every household.Later, the SDRF team led by Sangey Thinley imparted hands-on training in first aid, basic search and rescue techniques and the proper use of search and rescue equipment. Demonstrations of various rescue equipment were followed by mock drills, providing participants with practical experience in responding effectively during emergency situations.The ongoing awareness and training programme has so far covered residents of Mago, Indian Army and Indo-Tibetan Border Police (ITBP) personnel stationed there, people from the Thingbu Hydel area, and residents of New Maling and Tongsheng villages.The team will further extend the awareness and capacity-building programme to other vulnerable downstream settlements, including Phonda, Chaksam, Grenkhar and Dungshengmang villages, to strengthen community preparedness and build a more resilient response mechanism for potential GLOF emergencies.The initiative underscores the importance of community awareness, early warning, preparedness and coordinated response in safeguarding lives and property in vulnerable high-altitude areas of Tawang district.Meanwhile, APSDMA, in collaboration with DDMA, Tawang, and SDRF, conducted another awareness programme at Chagzam village under Kyidphel Circle on Monday.Villagers living downstream of the Tawang Chhu were sensitised to the potential risks associated with GLOFs and advised to remain alert, particularly amid changing climatic conditions and the possibility of emergencies.The awareness campaign aims to sensitise vulnerable downstream communities about high-risk glacial lakes and strengthen community-level disaster preparedness.During the programme, senior officials and experts from APSDMA, DDMA and SDRF briefed villagers on the location, altitude and distance of identified high-risk glacial lakes, their potential impact on downstream settlements, and the importance of preparedness and timely response.ZPM Kyidphel Tenzin Yendra Monpa also joined the team in raising awareness among villagers and shared key information on GLOF risks.He appealed to people not to panic but to remain informed, vigilant and prepared, and to follow advisories issued by competent authorities during any emergency.

97.title: Meet Colonel Hemonto Panging: The 9 Para SF Legend Known as the ‘Genghis Khan of the Indian Army’
97.description: Colonel Hemonto Panging, SM & Bar (Retd.), is a decorated former Indian Army officer whose years with 9 Para (Special Forces) placed him at the heart of
97.text:
Colonel Hemonto Panging, SM & Bar (Retd.), is a decorated former Indian Army officer whose years with 9 Para (Special Forces) placed him at the heart of some of the most demanding counter-insurgency operations in Assam and Jammu & Kashmir. Known among military circles as the “Genghis Khan” or “Chengiz Khan of the Indian Army,” Panging built a formidable reputation through aggressive pursuit, night operations, close-quarter engagements and missions deep inside hostile territory.

The nickname reflected the reputation he developed during years of operational service rather than a title formally bestowed by the Army. Speaking about the image associated with him, Panging has summed up his outlook by saying that only terrorists had reason to fear him, while for his country he carried his “heart on his sleeve.” Decades after many of these operations took place, interviews and accounts from fellow servicemen have gradually brought his largely little-known military career into the public domain.

Colonel Panging hails from Namsing village near Pasighat in Arunachal Pradesh’s East Siang district. He grew up in a family with a tradition of service and studied at Sainik School Imphal, an institution that has produced numerous officers for the Armed Forces. He subsequently joined the National Defence Academy, initially as an Air Force cadet, before opting for the Army. At the Indian Military Academy, Dehradun, he also distinguished himself in boxing.

Panging was commissioned into the 10th Battalion of the Jammu and Kashmir Rifles in 1991. His early operational exposure came in Assam during the turbulent years of Operation Bajrang and Operation Rhino, when security forces were conducting intensive operations against the United Liberation Front of Asom. As a young officer, Panging became known for operating with small teams and, on occasions, pursuing militants with minimal support.

Accounts from this period describe him travelling deep into militant-dominated areas and conducting operations at extremely close range. In one widely recounted episode, he reportedly captured ULFA militants and brought one of them back tied to a bicycle. He has also recalled walking nearly 25 kilometres into a militant-infested area armed with a pistol before making contact and pursuing his target over several more kilometres.

His career took a decisive turn when he volunteered for 9 Para (Special Forces), one of the Indian Army’s most experienced Special Forces battalions. After completing the demanding probation required to earn the maroon beret, Panging began a phase of his career dominated by counter-terrorism operations in Jammu & Kashmir.

He served multiple tenures in the Kashmir Valley and adjoining areas, including Doda, during some of the most violent years of militancy. His contemporaries included several distinguished Special Forces officers, among them Major Sudhir Kumar Walia, Ashoka Chakra, Sena Medal & Bar, who would later become one of the most celebrated soldiers of 9 Para SF.

Among the operations associated with Panging was a major engagement in the Doda region involving a sizeable group of terrorists positioned in difficult mountainous terrain above the Chenab. While the main force approached from one direction, Panging and a small team reportedly infiltrated behind the group, opening another axis of attack. Several terrorists were killed during the initial engagement, while others attempted to escape through a gorge. Panging’s team pursued them through the difficult terrain and continued the engagement. His gallantry during operations in this period contributed to him being awarded the Sena Medal.

Another significant operation came in the Bafliaz sector in 1997, when his team recovered a shoulder-fired surface-to-air missile from terrorists. The weapon represented a serious threat to military aviation in the region. During the operation, five militants were reportedly killed, while Panging’s team suffered one fatal casualty and two personnel were wounded. He subsequently received a Chief of Army Staff Commendation.

One of the most remarkable operations associated with Colonel Panging reportedly took place across the Line of Control in 1997. As a Major with 9 Para SF, he led a team several kilometres across the LoC during a night mission targeting a terrorist launch pad. The team infiltrated into hostile territory, struck the target and returned after an engagement lasting roughly an hour. Accounts of the mission state that around 20 terrorists were neutralised. Operations of this nature were rarely discussed publicly at the time, particularly when they involved Special Forces operating across the LoC.

Panging has also spoken about numerous other missions, including night contacts, ambushes, operations in dense terrain and the recovery of fallen soldiers under hostile fire. One operation he has referred to as the Shahji mission remains particularly significant to him because of how close he came to losing his life.

By the late 1990s, Indian forces in Jammu & Kashmir were increasingly confronting better-trained and more heavily armed militants. Panging has recalled the changing nature of the threat, including militants receiving increasingly sophisticated training and support from across the border. For Special Forces units such as 9 Para SF, this meant adapting tactics continuously while conducting prolonged counter-terrorism operations in extremely challenging terrain.

Over roughly a decade of operations in Jammu & Kashmir, Panging became associated with the elimination of a significant number of terrorists. Precise operational tallies have not been officially published in the public domain, and many details surrounding Special Forces missions from that period remain classified or available only through personal accounts.

His service eventually earned him the Sena Medal twice, giving him the distinction of SM & Bar. He later commanded 1 Assam Rifles, taking his years of operational experience back to the Northeast, where his military career had begun.

One of the most important relationships of Panging’s Special Forces career was with Major Sudhir Kumar Walia. Walia, an officer of 9 Para SF, was killed in action in Kupwara in August 1999 and was posthumously awarded the Ashoka Chakra. Panging has described Walia as one of the finest soldiers he ever served alongside and has spoken about his extraordinary patience, fieldcraft and mastery of weapons.

According to Panging, Walia could remain concealed for extraordinarily long periods while waiting for militants to reveal themselves, displaying the patience and discipline demanded by Special Forces operations. Panging has also reportedly been working on a book about Walia, preserving the story of an officer whose courage remains deeply respected within the Indian Army.

The “Genghis Khan” nickname attached to Panging was ultimately rooted in his operational style. He favoured infiltration, relentless pursuit and decisive engagement, even when the terrain or tactical situation made continuation difficult. His reputation became such that his name reportedly became shorthand among colleagues for an uncompromising approach to counter-terrorism operations.

For Panging, however, Special Forces service was about far more than aggression. He has repeatedly emphasised mental conditioning, initiative, physical endurance and the ability to make decisions independently under extreme pressure. He believes Special Forces training fundamentally changes the way a soldier approaches a problem, producing what he describes as a different kind of mental mobility.

Even after decades of demanding service, his attachment to 9 Para SF remains unmistakable. Panging has said that if he were given another life, he would once again choose the Indian Army and once again volunteer for 9 Para Special Forces.

Following retirement from the Army, Colonel Hemonto Panging turned his attention to another demanding pursuit: golf. He has competed at the senior amateur level and represented India at an international tournament in Haiphong, Vietnam, in 2024. The former Special Forces officer has also begun appearing in long-form interviews and public interactions where he discusses military life, leadership, counter-insurgency and the mindset required of a Special Forces soldier.

He has maintained a particularly strong connection with Arunachal Pradesh and has encouraged young people from the Northeast to consider careers in the Armed Forces. In March 2025, he interacted with cadets at Sainik School East Siang, returning to the region where his own journey towards military service had begun decades earlier.

For much of Colonel Panging’s career, details of his operations remained largely confined to the Special Forces fraternity and military circles in the Northeast. Accounts published by fellow servicemen and relatives, followed by a series of interviews in recent years, have gradually provided a broader picture of the officer behind the nickname.

From Sainik School Imphal and the National Defence Academy to 10 JAK Rifles, counter-insurgency operations in Assam and the maroon beret of 9 Para SF, Colonel Hemonto Panging’s career was shaped by some of the Indian Army’s toughest operational environments. Two Sena Medals, years of counter-terrorism operations and a reputation built among both comrades and adversaries made him one of the distinctive Special Forces personalities of his generation.

Today, the soldier once known for pursuing terrorists through mountains and across hostile territory can often be found on a golf course or speaking to younger generations. Yet the identity forged during his years with 9 Para SF remains central to his story — that of an officer from a small village in Arunachal Pradesh who earned the maroon beret and became known in military circles by an unforgettable name: the “Genghis Khan of the Indian Army.”

100.title: Meet Colonel Hemonto Panging: 9 Para SF Officer Known as the Genghis Khan of the Indian Army
100.description: Colonel Hemonto Panging, SM & Bar (Retd.), is among the most formidable counter-insurgency officers to have served in the Indian Army’s 9 Para (Special Forces). Over a decade of operations in A...
100.text:
Colonel Hemonto Panging, SM & Bar (Retd.), is among the most formidable counter-insurgency officers to have served in the Indian Army’s 9 Para (Special Forces). Over a decade of operations in Assam and Jammu & Kashmir, he earned a reputation so uncompromising that terrorists and fellow soldiers alike came to know him as the “Genghis Khan” or “Chengiz Khan” of the Indian Army.

The moniker was not a media invention. It grew from a record of close-quarter actions, night raids, lone pursuits and cross-border missions that left little room for negotiation. In recent years, long-form interviews have brought his previously little-known operational history into public view. The officer himself has summarised his stance with characteristic brevity: “If you want to fear me, you must be a terrorist. For my nation, I carry my heart on my sleeve.”

Origins in East Siang

Colonel Panging hails from Namsing village near Pasighat in East Siang district, Arunachal Pradesh. He belongs to a family with a strong tradition of national service. A relative, Group Captain (Retd.) M. Panging Pao of the Indian Air Force, recorded some of his operations in The Arunachal Times in 2020. Another family member, Mohonto Panging Pao, an erstwhile fighter pilot, later congratulated him when he represented India in senior amateur golf.

He studied at Sainik School Imphal. At the National Defence Academy he entered as an Air Force cadet but switched to the Army because his elder brother was already a pilot. At the Indian Military Academy he boxed and recorded a knockout. He has said he knew from school days that he was “made for the Fauj.” In March 2025 he returned to the region to address cadets at Sainik School East Siang.

His mother was a teacher. His wife is a doctor. They have a daughter, Kiara, described as an academic high-achiever, and a son who plays golf. His parents are deceased. He has spoken of himself as a committed father as well as a soldier.

Infantry Years: 10 JAK Rifles and Assam

He was commissioned in 1991 into the 10th Battalion of the Jammu and Kashmir Rifles. Early postings took him to Assam during Operation Bajrang and Operation Rhino against the United Liberation Front of Asom. As a young officer he conducted lone operations, including the capture of two ULFA leaders; one account describes him bringing a militant back tied to a bicycle. He has also described walking nearly 25 kilometres into a militant-infested area armed only with a pistol, making contact at close range and pursuing the target for several more kilometres.

These early years established a pattern that later defined his Special Forces service: initiative, physical endurance and a willingness to operate ahead of the main body.

The Maroon Beret: 9 Para SF

Around 1995 he volunteered for 9 Para (Special Forces) and completed the unit’s exacting probation. 9 Para SF is one of the Army’s oldest and most operationally experienced Special Forces battalions, with a long record in Jammu & Kashmir. He has described the transition from regular infantry as a change in how one thinks, acts and trains.

He served multiple tenures in the Kashmir theatre, including Doda, during some of the most violent years of the insurgency. Colleagues from that period included officers such as Major Paramjit Singh Sangha and, most notably, Major Sudhir Kumar Walia, AC, SM & Bar, later known as the “Rambo of the Indian Army.”

Operations That Defined a Reputation

Two Sena Medals for gallantry mark the publicly documented core of his record.

Doda, 1993 (first Sena Medal, as Captain). A group of 20–25 terrorists was operating from a mountain hideout above the Chenab. While the main force advanced from below, a small team under Captain Panging infiltrated behind them. The team killed three terrorists in the opening assault. The remainder fled into a gorge. Panging’s team pursued and killed seven more, including two foreign terrorists. The action was regarded as a major success for the Army in Doda that year.

Bafliaz, 1997. His team captured the first shoulder-fired surface-to-air missile then held by terrorists in the area, killed five militants and thereby prevented a possible strike on Indian aircraft. The team suffered one fatal casualty and two wounded. He received a Chief of Army Staff commendation.

Cross-border night raid, 1997 (second Sena Medal, as Major). He led a 9 Para SF team across the Line of Control approximately four to five kilometres into Pakistan-occupied Kashmir and attacked a terrorist launch pad beside a village. The night operation lasted about one hour and neutralised some 20 terrorists. Contemporaries have noted that such missions were not then publicly described as surgical strikes.

Other operations he has discussed include the Shahji mission, which he has called one of the most significant of his career and during which he came close to death; walnut-tree ambushes; night contacts in 1996; recovery of bodies under fire; and actions against increasingly professional militants trained by the ISI and Pakistan’s Special Services Group after 1997. He later commanded 1 Assam Rifles, drawing on his Northeast experience.

Over roughly ten years in Jammu & Kashmir he was credited with the elimination of a large number of terrorists. Exact official tallies are not published in open sources, which is typical for Special Forces service.

Brotherhood and Major Sudhir Walia

Colonel Panging has spoken at length about Major Sudhir Kumar Walia, who was killed in action in Kupwara in August 1999 and posthumously awarded the Ashoka Chakra. He has described Walia as the finest soldier he served with—a man whose weapon was an extension of himself and who would sit for two days on a thin wooden roof waiting for militants. A book by Panging on Walia has been reported as under preparation. The association places Panging within a small circle of 9 Para SF officers whose operational years in the mid-1990s remain a reference point inside the unit.

Why “Genghis Khan”

The nickname reflected method as much as results. Panging favoured infiltration, pursuit into difficult ground and rapid, decisive contact. Fellow officers reportedly used his name as shorthand when a situation required an uncompromising response. He has said that action matters more than words and that Special Forces training produces a different mental mobility. He has also stated that if born again he would join the Army and 9 Para SF once more.

After Service

Colonel Panging is retired. As of interviews recorded in 2025 and 2026 he described himself as recently retired. He now competes in senior amateur golf and represented India at an international tournament in Haiphong, Vietnam, in 2024. He appears in extended conversations on channels such as Monks & Warriors and The Syllabus of Life, and he addresses young cadets on discipline, patriotism and service. His public presence is modest: an Instagram account under the handle @colpanging, with the description “9 PARA I Golfer I SF Mindset.”

He has used those platforms to speak about Arunachal Pradesh’s record of military service and to encourage young people, particularly from the Northeast, to consider the armed forces.

A Record That Remained Quiet for Years

For much of his career, Colonel Panging’s operations were known mainly within the Special Forces community and in parts of Arunachal Pradesh. The 2020 article by Group Captain Panging Pao and the wave of interviews from 2025 onward have made the outline of that record available to a wider audience. Official gazette citations and complete posting particulars remain limited in the public domain, as is customary for officers of his background.

What is clear is the shape of the career: Sainik School and NDA; commissioning into 10 JAK Rifles in 1991; early combat in Assam; the maroon beret of 9 Para SF; two Sena Medals; a decade of counter-insurgency in Kashmir; and a reputation that terrorists themselves helped create. The officer from Namsing village became, for a generation of operators and adversaries, a name that meant the pursuit would not stop at the gorge or at the Line of Control.

101.title: Indian Army and Monica Sarin Foundation Open Employment Pathways for Dooars Youth Through Project Yuva Shakti
101.description: Indian Army backed initiative connects youth from remote border villages to employment opportunities in Delhi
101.text:
Indian Army backed initiative connects youth from remote border villages to employment opportunities in Delhi

New Delhi : In a collaborative effort to expand employment opportunities for youth from remote border communities, the Indian Army and Monica Sarin Foundation (MSF) have launched Project Yuva Shakti, an initiative designed to provide industry-linked skill development and exposure to young people from the Dooars area in the north-eastern region of India. The programme commenced on August 25, 2026 enabling the first cohort of select 10 participants, including four young women travelling to Delhi for skill development and training across hospitality, healthcare and retail sectors.

-- Advertisement --

The initiative seeks to address the limited access to career opportunities faced by many young people in the Dooars, a region where a significant proportion of families continue to depend on tea plantation-based livelihoods. Through industry-oriented training, workplace exposure and mentorship, Project Yuva Shakti aims to improve participants’ employability and future readiness for long-term careers.

Aashman Sarin, Director and Founding Member, Monica Sarin Foundation, said, “Talent exists everywhere but opportunities often do not. Through Project Yuva Shakti, we are working to bridge that gap by making an effort to connect young people from the remote Dooars region with industry relevant skills, exposure and pathways to employment. Our partnership with the Indian Army enables us to reach communities where such opportunities are often limited.

Commenting on the partnership, an Army Spokesperson also said, “Empowering youth of remote border areas like that of the Dooar region, is integral to our commitment towards inclusive development and nation-building. Project Yuva Shakti seeks to equip young people from the region with skills, confidence and exposure needed to pursue meaningful careers and contribute positively to their communities.”

-- Advertisement --

Project Yuva Shakti is bult on Monica Sarin Foundation’s broader skilling initiatives through the Monica Sarin Centre for Advanced Skills, Innovation and Entrepreneurship (MS-CASIE), which has trained over 380 young people, with more than 299 transitioning to employment or entrepreneurial opportunities, as on September 22, 2026.

The project comes at a time when studies have highlighted persistent livelihood vulnerabilities among tea plantation communities in the Dooars and Darjeeling regions, including low incomes, employment insecurity and limited opportunities for youth. Against this backdrop, the initiative seeks to create pathways to industry-linked skills and sustainable employment for young people from underserved communities. For participants such as Snigdha Sharma, a Class XII graduate from the Dooars, the programme represents an opportunity to gain exposure beyond her immediate surroundings and work towards greater financial independence and long-term career aspirations.

102.title: Assam Rifles holds security meetings with civil society groups in Manipur's Jiribam
102.description: Assam Rifles held security meetings with civil society groups at Borobekra and NKP in Jiribam on September 22. The talks stressed neutral community support, dialogue and trust-building to restore normalcy.
102.text:
Assam Rifles conducted security meetings with representatives of Civil Society Organisations (CSOs) at Borobekra and NKP in Manipur’s Jiribam district on September 22 to discuss the prevailing security situation and measures to strengthen peace and stability in the region.

The meetings were attended by the DIG, 21 Sector Assam Rifles, Commandant, 38 Assam Rifles, and other officers. Discussions focused on strengthening coordination among security forces, civil society and local stakeholders to promote peace and stability.

At NKP, representatives of the Kuki and Naga communities also participated in the meeting. Chairpersons, secretaries and other representatives from NKP, Tatbung, Muktakhal, Pangmol, OKP and Kulbung villages attended the discussions.

The meeting emphasised the importance of peaceful coexistence, mutual trust and confidence-building between the two communities at the grassroots level.

Assam Rifles urged all stakeholders to maintain a neutral environment conducive to peace and stability and refrain from extending any support or assistance to armed cadres.

The engagements also highlighted the importance of community participation, sustained dialogue and close coordination between security forces and civil society in efforts to maintain peace, restore normalcy and strengthen stability in Jiribam.

103.title: Chief of banned Manipur-based UKNA militant outfit arrested in Mizoram
103.description: Security forces on September 24 arrested the alleged commander-in-chief of the banned Manipur-based United Kuki National Army (UKNA) in Mizoram's capital Aizawl, a senior police officer said.
103.text:
Security forces on September 24 arrested the alleged commander-in-chief of the banned Manipur-based United Kuki National Army (UKNA) in Mizoram's capital Aizawl, a senior police officer said.

Thangkhomang Haokip, who is stated to be the chief of the UKNA, was arrested during a joint operation by the Assam Rifles and the Subsidiary Intelligence Bureau (SIB), Aizawl Superintendent of Police Zosangliana said.

An official of a central intelligence agency said security forces were also conducting searches for other cadres of the banned outfit who are reportedly hiding in Aizawl.

Officials in Imphal said the UKNA is not a signatory to the Suspension of Operations (SoO) agreement, which was signed between the Centre, the Manipur government and several Kuki and Zomi militant groups.

The outfit is primarily active in the hill district of Churachandpur, particularly in the Henglep subdivision, officials said.

The arrest comes weeks after the National Investigation Agency (NIA) arrested S Palal Thadou, the self-styled finance head of the proscribed UKNA, in connection with an April 7 IED blast in Manipur's Bishnupur district that killed two children.

The ethnic conflict between the valley-based Meitei and hill-based Kuki communities, which erupted in May 2023, has claimed at least 306 lives, while 49 people remain missing and thousands have been displaced, according to official figures cited in the report.

104.title: Eastern Army Commander discusses Manipur with Spear Corps, Assam Rifles officers
104.description: Apart from stepping up operations to seize weapons and apprehend militants, the Assam Rifles has taken measures to reach out to civilian leadership in an effort to end the conflict.
104.text:
Kolkata: Lt Gen VMB Krishnan, General Officer Commanding-in-Chief (GOC-in-C), Eastern Command, met senior officers of Spear Corps and Assam Rifles units in Manipur to assess the state's situation. Ethnic clashes continue in parts of Manipur, with incidents of deaths and arson being reported.

The latest casualty was a Kuki man killed on Wednesday morning, after which nearly 24 houses in two Naga villages were set ablaze. The killing was in retaliation for the death of a Naga youth a day earlier. Four people, including three women, had been killed a few days before. The latest violence was concentrated in the hill districts of Kangpokpi and Tamenglong.

Militant outfits such as the NSCN(IM) and Kuki National Army are involved in the violence. The Assam Rifles, along with other security forces, are attempting to end the conflict that has rocked the state for over three years, claiming more than 306 lives. Several people remain missing, and thousands are displaced, living in makeshift camps.

A senior official said, “The Eastern Army Commander held detailed discussions with officers on strategies adopted and outcomes. He also interacted with troops, some of whom received commendation cards and medals.”

Apart from stepping up operations to seize weapons and apprehend militants, the Assam Rifles has taken measures to reach out to civilian leadership in an effort to end the conflict. Senior officers convened a meeting with Naga and Kuki-Zo community leaders a few days ago, urging them to adopt a neutral stance to stop the violence that is hampering the state’s development.

The violence initially began between the majority Meiteis, who occupy the valley districts, and the Kukis from the hills. The spark was an attempt by Hindu Meiteis to seek Scheduled Tribe (ST) status on par with the Kukis so that they could gain control over forest land. Despite being fewer in number, the Kukis control more land than the Meiteis, with ST status enabling them to claim forest land.

The Meiteis have accused the Kuki-Zos of illegal infiltration and narco-terrorism. While a barrier has now emerged between the Meiteis and Kukis, violence has spread to the hills, with clashes between Nagas and Kukis. The primary cause is land occupation.

The Nagas make up nearly 20 per cent of Manipur’s population and are the second-largest ethnic group after the Meiteis. Initially aloof during Meitei-Kuki clashes, the Nagas became involved after Kukis attempted to take control of villages.

The Meiteis have now forced the government to withhold census operations in the state. They have demanded a National Register of Citizens (NRC) to weed out illegal immigrants.

105.title: 4 Naga civilians killed near Indo-Myanmar border in Manipur; shutdown called
105.description: The incident occurred on Thursday evening when suspected KNA-B militants, armed with sophisticated weapons, entered Pilong Naga village and opened fire on villagers, the police said.
105.text:
Condemning the killings, the Tangkhul Naga Long called a 24-hour emergency shutdown across its jurisdiction from 7 am Friday. (Representational image)

Four Tangkhul Naga civilians, including a father and son, were allegedly killed after suspected Myanmar-based Kuki National Army-Burma (KNA-B) militants attacked a village in Manipur’s Kamjong district, the police said.

According to the police, the incident occurred on Thursday evening when suspected KNA-B militants, armed with sophisticated weapons, entered Pilong Naga village and opened fire on villagers, killing four civilians.

Pilong Naga village is located along the India-Myanmar border, around 35 km from the Kamjong district headquarters. With the latest incident, at least eight people have been killed in separate incidents over the past nearly two weeks involving members of the Naga and Kuki-Zo communities.

106.title: Indian Military: Portent of Adversarial Defeat Owing to Lackadaisical attitude of the BJP
106.description: By Melarbor L Thabah When I was in my late teenage years till present, I have always been passionate about
106.text:
By Melarbor L Thabah

When I was in my late teenage years till present, I have always been passionate about defence issues. In this current state, should a war break out between China and India, the Indian Air Force and Navy will be totally obliterated by the Chinese Air Force and Navy because of politico-bureaucratic red tape, slow reforms, limited funding and delayed local manufacturing which slows down large-scale procurement, and advanced weapons manufacturing. A brief glance on the respective shortcomings of each branch of the tri services is indispensable.

Shortcomings of the Indian AirForce:

India has an ageing fleet of aircrafts coupled with slow replacements since the retirement of the infamous pilot killer MiG 21. India faces a severe aircraft crisis with only 30 squadrons left from the minimum 42 and the maximum 70 squadrons that it must have in the event of a two-front war against China and Pakistan. India mostly has 4th and 3rd Generation fighter jets which will be difficult to combat the 5th generation fighter jets. These old jets will have to be phased out in the 2030s thus leaving India with a severely depleted Air Force. A strong Air Force is needed to protect North East India from China.

India has approximately 558 fighter and trainer jets compared to China which has 1,228 jets. The process of upgrading the existing jets is going nowhere. To add to this sordid state, Modi cancelled the purchase of 126 fighter jets in favour for only 36 Rafale fighter jets and the uncertain 83 Tejas jets of HAL, India, which the government had placed orders though the GE engines needed for Tejas jets are currently stalled by the USA. India’s AMCA programme of producing 5th generation fighter jets is still in the prototype and industry bidding phase.

In 2011, the IAF sent a proposal to the defence ministry to increase its sanctioned fighter aircraft strength to 45 combat squadrons to be readily prepared for war but received a poor response from the government. For decades, India has had a very poor rate of inducting new fighter aircraft with no off-the-shelf foreign procurements planned. Air Chief Marshal AP Singh recently highlighted the severe crisis in the Indian Air Force warning that the IAF is struggling to maintain its operational edge, making it imperative to fast-track acquisitions and plug equipment shortfall. Indian governments including this incumbent one has a knack for wasteful public expenditure by forming needless committees rather than trusting its officers. Nonetheless, the committee formed reported that the crisis is grave. Even then, the political leadership did not act by rapidly procuring en masse to meet these exigencies.

Analytical Air Force comparative approximates: Aircraft number between India and China are ;10 Reconnaissance Aircrafts compared to China which has 48, 3 Electronic Warfare Aircrafts versus China’s 35, 7 Tanker Aircrafts versus China’s 26, 179 important Unmanned Ariel Vehicles versus China’s 350, 594 Helicopters versus China’s 913, 79 Attack Helicopters versus China’s 281, 281 Transport Aircrafts versus China’s 295, 0 Helicopter Carriers, 72 Special Mission Aircraft versus China’s 419, 0 Long Range Bomber Aircrafts versus China’s 125 and most importantly 0 critical Fifth Generation stealth Fighter Jets versus China’s 560. Despite the offer from Russia, India refused to purchase 5th Generation fighter jets. Parliamentary Law is needed so that India will compulsorily have at least sixty squadrons because of the two-war front scenario.

Shortcomings of the Indian Navy:

India has a vast coastline with an Exclusive Economic Zone of 370 KMs encompassing innumerable strategic islands especially in the Bay of Bengal. Yet, previous and current governments have taken minute steps for naval modernization. The Indian Navy suffers from a shrinking submarine fleet, aging boats, submarines running on old technology with delayed upgrades, manpower shortages including officers, sailors and civilian workers for repairs. Most conventional diesel-electric submarines are over 30 years old with defects detected like in 26 Scorpene submarines. Lack of Air-Independent Propulsion disables submarines to stay longer underwater. India operates fewer submarines than its target number. Projected 75 submarine plans are progressing at a snail’s pace. Indian Navy’s premier destroyers and frigates use two totally incompatible Vertical Launch Systems for different missiles compared to other advanced nations which launch different missile varieties from the same cell.

Analytical Naval comparative approximates: Naval variant number between India and China are; 20 Frigates of India versus China’s 59, 13 Destroyers versus China’s 62, 23 Corvettes versus China’s 62, 16 Diesel Electric Submarines versus China’s 46, 3 Nuclear Submarines versus China’s 16, 290 naval aircrafts versus China’s 700, 0 mine counter vessel versus China’s 37, 2 Aircraft Carriers versus China’s 3, 5 amphibious vessels versus China’s 81, 0 Unmanned Vehicles versus China’s 34 and 13 ports versus China’s 22.

Shortcomings of the Indian Army:

It faces critical institutional shortcomings, slow procurement cycles, short supplies of basic ammunitions – fuses and infrastructure deficits along its borders. Many major weapon systems and equipment lag state-of-the-art technology required to outmatch advanced adversaries. Reports suggest a persistent shortage of thousands of officers against the sanctioned strength contiguous with heavy deployment for counter-insurgency and internal security obligations pulls the focus away from conventional high-intensity warfare preparedness.

Analytical Army comparative approximates: Army machines number between India and China are; 4,200 Indian tanks versus China’s 6,800, 264 MRLS versus China’s 2,750, 350 Ballistic missiles versus China’s 1,300, 1,000 drones versus China’s 4,500, 100 Self Propelled Artillery versus China’s 3,090, 100 Rocket Projectile Vehicles versus China’s 2,770, 2,415 Infantry vehicle versus China’s 8,050, 1,730 Armoured Carrier Vehicles versus China’s 4,350 and 1,730 MRAP versus China’s 3,768.

Overarching Ubiquitous Deficiencies of the Tri Services are:

Infrastructure, Logistics, Procurement Delays: – Red tape hurdles, slow infrastructural development, transportations, acquisition of advanced weapon systems and military hardware.

Equipment Modernization and Mass Manufacturing – Sluggishness in modernization, technological mass production of machines and equipment caused severe roadblocks with miniature indigenization progress.

Budgetary Constraints: 60% of India’s defence budget is consumed by salaries, pensions and unnecessary civil works thereby leaving inadequate funds for procurement.

Institutional Silos: The Tri Services have traditionally operated in separate silos with limited joint warfare coordination.

Procurement, R&D Lags, Oil Reserves: Procurement plagues major domestic programs like the Tejas fighter jet engine and the indigenous Arjun tank development. Research and Development has stalled in various technological fields. Oil reserves for running the machines of the Tri Services is not sufficient with only 21 million barrels of stored oil reserves lacking huge constructed hidden reserves for oil storage compared to China which has 1.4 billion barrels of stored oil with first priority to its Tri Services.

Unified Commands: China has five Unified Commands while India has only two fully functional Tri-Service unified commands of the army, navy, and air force assets which are not yet fully integrated theatre commands under the theaterization reform. Plans are moving at a snail’s pace to merge Northern, Western, and Maritime commands. Currently, 17 single-service commands (7 Army, 7 Air Force, 3 Navy) are not yet integrated.

Overall assessment analysis: Comparisons with China are majorly imperative so that India can have a benchmark to know in which state India is in when compared with its dangerous yet advanced adversary in order to achieve the desired technological modernisation and restructuring needed for stellar defence from which China will serve as the main benchmark. India’s military budget of only 86 billion is decent compared to the size and geography of the nation. It should be increased to be spent more on technology with 51% from the defence budget because as the world progresses, reliance on technology to win wars has become more pivotal not discounting personnel contribution. Current insanely humongous personnel number in the army implies more surrender. The low number of personnel types in the Air Force and Navy can be supplemented by converting one hundred thousand retired army posts to the Air Force and Navy respectively to supplement personnel shortage in these two services which will not be a problem since India has approximately 1.48 million active and 1.15 million reserve duty military personnel. The share of GDP ratio to the defence budget must be increased. The haughty conjectural nationalistic argument about the effectiveness of Chinese technology being untested in war must not be underestimated as they may be actually effective in a war. I appreciate the various reforms which the current ruling depensation has undertaken. I exhort the government to simplify the various paramilitary forces by subsuming the ITBP and SSB under the BSF and the Assam Rifles under the NSG. India must exhibit utmost urgency to buy weapons immediately to supplement the shortage in the tri services. In doing so, the urgent needs of the military are met whilst allowing time for its fledgling domestic military industry to grow. The government has to take cognizance that India faces an extreme threat from China and Pakistan which is why rapid modernization, mass manufacturing and structural reforms is requisite. A militarily strong nation commands immense respect and deters foes.

107.title: ‘Northeast is not where India ends, but where India begins’: Gen Upendra Dwivedi in Guwahati
107.description: Former Chief of Army Staff General Upendra Dwivedi (Retd) on September 25 described the Northeast as a "true gateway" to India, calling on young people to combine technological skills with adaptability, ability and a strong grounding in Indian values.
107.text:
Former Chief of Army Staff General Upendra Dwivedi (Retd) on September 25 described the Northeast as a "true gateway" to India, calling on young people to combine technological skills with adaptability, ability and a strong grounding in Indian values.

Dwivedi was speaking at 'Namami Bharatam', a collective singing programme organised by Vidya Bharati Northeast Region at the Srimanta Sankaradeva International Auditorium in Guwahati to mark the 150th anniversary of Vande Mataram.

Addressing the gathering, Dwivedi said, "The Northeast is not the place where India ends, but the place from where India begins. It is the true gateway to the nation."

He said he was addressing the gathering not merely as a former Army chief but as an alumnus of Saraswati Shishu Mandir, and urged students to play an active role in nation-building.

Dwivedi called upon young people to focus on three pillars — attitude, adaptability and ability — as India works towards the goal of becoming a developed nation by 2047.

Urging students to become solution providers rather than merely identifying problems, he encouraged them to follow a continuous process of "learn, unlearn and relearn". He also stressed the need for young people to understand emerging technologies while remaining rooted in Indian values.

Dwivedi suggested a daily 'Zero-Ten' routine, asking young people to spend the first 10 minutes of every morning away from mobile phones, using the time to focus on their goals, express gratitude and set their intentions for the day.

The event brought together students, educators, alumni and members of civil society for a synchronised rendition of Vande Mataram. Vidya Bharati Northeast organisational secretary Dr Pawan Tiwari said the national song represented India's cultural unity and highlighted the Northeast's historical and cultural contributions.

Tiwari referred to the spiritual legacy of Maa Kamakhya and Srimanta Sankaradeva, as well as the military history associated with Ahom general Lachit Borphukan, while speaking about the region's place in India's national consciousness.

The programme was attended by Air Vice Marshal Sanjeev Bordoloi (Retd), Dr Jagadindra Ray Choudhury, Shishu Shiksha Samiti Assam president Kulendra Kumar Bhagwati, programme coordinator Gaurav Kalita and Assam Gaurav awardee Meenakshi Das, among others.

Speaking to reporters, Vidya Bharati Assam media architect Sailendra Pandey said the collective singing from Assam highlighted the Northeast's role in India's cultural and strategic landscape.

The event marked the 150th anniversary of India's national song, Vande Mataram, and was attended by Air Vice Marshal Sanjeev Bordoloi (Retd), Pawan Tiwari (Organisational Secretary, Vidya Bharati Northeast), Jagadindra Ray Choudhury, Kulendra Kumar Bhagwati (President, Shishu Shiksha Samiti Assam), Program Coordinator Gaurav Kalita, and Assam Gaurav recipient Meenakshi Das. News india Op Fortress Siliguri: India Takes Underground Route To Secure Chicken’s Neck | Exclusive

Op Fortress Siliguri: India Takes Underground Route To Secure Chicken’s Neck | Exclusive

Reported By :

, Edited By:



Last Updated: September 25, 2026, 19:46 IST

Rapid Read

The Siliguri Corridor — India’s narrow land link to the Northeast — is witnessing a major infrastructure push. (File for representation)

PM Narendra Modi-led government is moving critical military infrastructure, transport capacity and border connectivity underground and across multiple parallel routes to secure the Siliguri Corridor. CNN-News18 decodes the emerging security architecture around India’s strategic eastern chokepoint — from underground military infrastructure and proposed rail connectivity to six-lane highways, border roads and new military stations.

The Siliguri Corridor — India’s narrow land link to the Northeast — is witnessing a major infrastructure push. Government plans and projects spanning the Army, Railways, Ministry of Road Transport and Highways, Home Ministry and border forces point towards a layered approach – more routes, more redundancy and greater protection for critical military and civilian infrastructure.

The objective, according to government planning, is to reduce dependence on individual surface routes and strengthen the resilience of the corridor in a crisis.

1. Underground ammunition and defence stockpiling for Indian army

Construction of 12 Underground Army Air Defence (AAD) Ammunition Storage facilities, 1 Underground Long Range Vector (LRV) Ammunition Storage (SMERCH), and 21 over-ground LRV emplacements (total cost): ₹297 Crore

This is needed to store heavy air defence and long-range vector ammunition underground protects critical military assets against preemptive aerial strikes or drone attacks in a narrow geographical chokepoint

2. Command, control and protective fortification for Indian Army

At A Glance 1 . The government is constructing 12 Underground Army Air Defence (AAD) Ammunition Storage facilities, 1 Underground Long Range Vector (LRV) Ammunition Storage, and 21 over-ground LRV emplacements for ₹297 Crore. 2 . Plans include 5 Underground Command & Control Centres, 6 Underground Communication Centres, 2 Critical Storage Spaces, 3 Underground LRV Ammunition Storages, and 12 Bomb Shelters for ₹237 Crore. 3 . The Siliguri Corridor Underground Railway Tunnel is being executed alongside double-laning of the NJP Siliguri and Thakurgan–Siliguri railway tracks. 4 . Construction includes the Six-Lane Gorakhpur–Siliguri Expressway, a Six-Lane road bridge, a Siliguri Ring Road, and four-laning of NH 27 and NH 17. 5 . 75 km out of 79.5 km of the Fatehpur to Galgalia border road under the INBR project is near completion. Show More

Govt is Planning 5 Underground Command & Control Centres, 6 Underground Communication Centres, 2 Critical Storage Spaces, 3 Underground LRV Ammunition Storages, and 12 Bomb Shelters: ₹237 Crore under AMWP

Subterranean command and signal nodes ensure uninterrupted military operational control and survivability during electronic warfare or high-intensity bombardments

3. Subsurface Rail capacity and double laning (Ministry of Railways)

Execution of the Siliguri Corridor Underground Railway Tunnel alongside double-laning of the NJP Siliguri and Thakurganj–Siliguri railway tracks

This is helping in expanding railway infrastructure and moving tracks underground mitigates bottleneck risks and ensures resilient supply chains for both civil movement and rapid defense mobilization into the Northeast.

4. Ring Roads and Multi-Lane Highway Arteries (MoRTH)

Construction of the Six-Lane Gorakhpur–Siliguri Expressway, a Six-Lane road bridge (alternate to Coronation Bridge), a Siliguri Ring Road, and four-laning and upgradation of NH 27 and NH 17.

This will eliminate single-point traffic failures, bypasses urban congestion, and drastically speeds up inter-state transit times between North and Central India and the eastern border

5. Critical lateral links and strategic upgrades (MoRTH)

Upgradation of 3 lateral routes connecting NH 17 and NH 27, alongside upgrading NH 10 (Sevoke–Rangpo) to NHDL (PS) heavy-load defence specifications

This is helpful in strengthening NH 10 and lateral links provides backup redundancy for heavy military transport vehicles heading toward Sikkim and border defence sectors.

6. Indo-Nepal Border Transit Development (SSB)

Near completion (75 km out of 79.5 km) of the Fatehpur to Galgalia border road under the INBR project, with additional proposals for Indo-Nepal Border Road-II submitted to the MHA.

This secures and regulates the open border with Nepal, preventing illegal infiltration, cross-border smuggling, and ensuring rapid patrol access for border guarding forces.

7. Integrated Bhutan Linkages & Defensive Basing (MHA & AHQ)

Submission of proposals for Indo-Bhutan Border Road-I (incorporating Siliguri Corridor sections) and ongoing plans by Army Headquarters (AHQ) to establish new Military Stations in the corridor.

This secures key access points near the tri-junction and Doklam region, expanding static troop presence to react swiftly to tactical developments

WHAT GOVT SOURCES SAY

The Government of India is transitioning from basic surface infrastructure to a dual-use subterranean and multi-modal transit network, say sources.

By moving ammunition, command centres, and railway lines underground, the corridor moves away from being a vulnerable single point of failure to a fortress-like logistics hub.

Given the narrow 22 km width of the Siliguri Corridor-Chicken’s Neck sandwiched between international borders, building parallel expressways, underground railways, and fortified border roads prevents potential blockades and ensures the Northeast remains permanently connected to mainland India, they say.

Moving critical command and control centres, signal networks, railway transit, and heavy air defence ammunition underground of more than Rs 500 crore in Army projects marks a total shift in defence architecture, say sources.

Upgrading NH 10 to heavy load NHDL specifications, completing the Indo-Nepal Border Road -Fatehpur to Galgalia and advancing the Indo-Bhutan border links provides seamless cross-corridor access for border security forces (SSB, BSF) and the Indian Army. Establishing new military stations near key access points drastically improves India’s reaction time to potential flashpoints along sensitive border zones like Doklam and the Sikkim tri-junction, they say.

The Indian government is fortifying the Siliguri Corridor by relocating critical military infrastructure, transport capacity, and border connectivity underground and across parallel routes. Key projects include 12 underground AAD ammunition storage facilities, 5 underground command and control centers, bomb shelters, a subsurface railway tunnel project, six-lane highways like the Gorakhpur–Siliguri Expressway, and upgraded border transit routes to ensure continuous connectivity to the Northeast. Why is the Siliguri Corridor considered a critical strategic chokepoint for India? Also known as the Chicken's Neck, the Siliguri Corridor is a slender 17 to 22-kilometer-wide land strip in West Bengal that serves as the sole terrestrial link connecting mainland India to its eight northeastern states. Because nearly all major rail, road, fuel, and military supply routes pass through this narrow passage sandwiched between international borders, it has historically been viewed as a vulnerable strategic chokepoint requiring enhanced defense resilience. How are rail and road networks being developed to improve mobility in the Siliguri Corridor? The Ministry of Railways is executing an underground railway tunnel and double-laning tracks to ensure resilient supply chains and rapid defense mobilization. Simultaneously, the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways (MoRTH) is constructing the Siliguri Ring Road, the six-lane Gorakhpur–Siliguri Expressway, an alternate road bridge to the Coronation Bridge, and upgrading NH 10 to heavy-load defense specifications to eliminate single-point traffic failures and speed up transit. India News | “Northeast Not Where India Ends, but Where India Begins”: Former COAS Gen Upendra Dwivedi .
111.text:
Guwahati (Assam) [India], September 25 (ANI): Former Chief of Army Staff General Upendra Dwivedi (Retd) on Friday attended a grand collective singing ceremony titled ‘Namami Bharatam’, which was convened at the Srimanta Sankaradeva International Auditorium, under the aegis of Vidya Bharati Northeast Region.

Expressing pride as an alumnus of Saraswati Shishu Mandir rather than a former military commander, General Upendra Dwivedi said, "The Northeast is not the place where India ends, but the place from where India begins. It is the true gateway to the nation."

Also Read | KPSC Job Scam: Bengaluru Court Denies Bail to Suspended IAS Officer Gyanendra Gangwar.

Frame Vande Mataram as the ultimate battle cry for a fully developed India by 2047, General Dwivedi called upon the youth to anchor their lives on three foundational pillars: Attitude, Adaptability, and Ability.

According to the press release, in a sharp directive to the younger generation, Gen Dwivedi urged students to abandon passive criticism and emerge as proactive solution-providers.

Also Read | Nagaland State Lottery Sambad Result Today 8 PM Live: Dear Horizon Friday Lottery Result of September 25, 2026 Declared Online, Watch Lucky Draw Winners List.

He championed the continuous cycle of “Learn, Unlearn, and Relearn,” urging the youth to master cutting-edge modern technology while staying fiercely rooted in core Indian values and courage

To cultivate mental clarity and purpose, Gen Dwivedi issued a practical challenge to the youth: adopt a daily ‘Zero-Ten’ rule—spending the first ten minutes of every morning completely disconnected from mobile phones to align with personal goals, express gratitude, and set daily intentions.

Media architect of Vidya Bharati Assam, Sailendra Pandey emphasised the transformative impact of the event, stating that the collective resonance of Vande Mataram from the sacred soil of Assam serves as a powerful reminder of the region's pivotal role in shaping India's cultural and strategic future.

Addressing the gathering, Pawan Tiwari underscored that Vande Mataram transcends being a mere anthem—it is the living pulse of India’s cultural oneness. He paid tribute to the Northeast’s spiritual and historic legacy, noting that the voice rising from the sacred land of Maa Kamakhya, the spiritual consciousness of Srimanta Sankaradeva, and the legendary valour of Bir Lachit Borphukan reinforce the indivisible integrity of the nation, according to the press release.

The event marked the 150th anniversary of India’s national song, Vande Mataram, and was attended by Air Vice Marshal Sanjeev Bordoloi (Retd), Pawan Tiwari (Organisational Secretary, Vidya Bharati Northeast), Jagadindra Ray Choudhury, Kulendra Kumar Bhagwati (President, Shishu Shiksha Samiti Assam), Program Coordinator Gaurav Kalita, and Assam Gaurav recipient Meenakshi Das. (ANI)
