134.title: From 3Cs to 7Cs: Counter Insurgency and Jungle Warfare school charts a people-centric roadmap for Northeast India
134.description: CIJW School, hosted a two-day seminar on cultural diplomacy, indigenous communities and people-centric engagement.
134.text:
GUWAHATI: Counter Insurgency and Jungle Warfare School, Vairengte, conducted a two-day seminar on “Cultural Diplomacy, Ecosystem of Tribals and Indigenous People, Population-Centric Engagement and Way Ahead for Northeast India” on September 23–24, 2026.

The seminar brought together eminent moderators and speakers from NIT Silchar, Assam University, Central University of Jharkhand, Mizoram University, North-Eastern Hill University, Tripura University, the Indian Institute of Public Administration, and DIPR, DRDO, along with army officers, academicians, and students. The three thematic sessions brought academic research, professional experience and local understanding onto a common platform.

The first thematic session, “Cultural Diplomacy & Ecosystem of Tribals and Indigenous People,” explored the cultural strengths of Northeast India and their potential for strengthening people-to-people linkages. The session discussed cultural diplomacy through food, hospitality, tourism, festivals, tea, textiles, language, and indigenous traditions, along with the Northeast’s potential to serve as a cultural bridge to India’s eastern neighbourhood. The discussion also examined tribal customs and indigenous practices across different communities and states, including the practical and scientific reasoning associated with several traditional practices. Meaningful participation of women in initiatives undertaken by institutions and organisations emerged as an important theme. The session also examined cross-border cultural and ethnic linkages through kinship, language, traditions, movement, and historical relationships.

The second thematic session, “Population-Centric Engagement,” placed trust at the centre of meaningful engagement with local populations. Deliberations highlighted the need for the Army, security forces and other institutions to understand existing community structures and engage through local associations, community organisations and their leadership. The session also highlighted the importance of cultural intelligence, strong kinship structures, and attachment to roots, with Mizoram providing a useful example of a closely connected and relatively non-hierarchical society. Contemporary challenges, particularly drug abuse, were discussed alongside changing youth aspirations and the need for greater involvement of digitally educated youth in government, institutional and community mechanisms.

The final thematic session, “Economic & Technological Pathways & Way Ahead,” focused on future development opportunities for the region. Participants analysed extensive comparative economic data and offered suggestions to strengthen Northeast India’s economic development. The technological dimension highlighted existing Government technology initiatives while also proposing new technology-enabled solutions to improve governance, accessibility, service delivery, and development outcomes.

A thought that resonated repeatedly through the seminar was the Vedic invocation “आ नो भद्राः क्रतवो यन्तु विश्वतः” — “Let noble thoughts come to us from every direction.” Emphasised by several speakers, it aptly reflected the spirit of the interaction—bringing together diverse disciplines, experiences and perspectives while remaining open to ideas from different directions.

An interesting progression of ideas also emerged through the two days. The discourse began with the 3 Cs — Connectivity, Culture and Community, emphasising that regional engagement must go beyond physical connectivity alone. As the discussion widened towards cross-border linkages and cooperation, the thought expanded to the 5 Cs — Culture, Community, Connectivity, Cooperation and Confidence. In his closing remarks, Maj Gen Kulvir Singh, SM, PhD, Commandant, CIJW School, carried this progression further into a comprehensive 7 Cs framework: Culture, Community, Connectivity, Capacity, Commerce, Confidence and Convergence. He also underscored inclusive growth and women’s meaningful participation as essential to shaping the way ahead for Northeast India.

This 3–5–7 progression captured the seminar’s broad journey—from cultural understanding and community engagement, through cooperation and confidence, to capacity building, economic opportunity, and convergence of efforts.

The seminar strengthened Army–academia interaction and generated practical perspectives towards an inclusive, people-centric and progressive future for Northeast India.

135.title: Sikkim CM highlights Newar community’s contribution to state at Indrajatra festival
135.description: Sikkim Chief Minister Prem Singh Tamang on Friday, September 25, highlighted the contribution of the Newar community to the state’s development, saying the Indrajatra festival embodies values of nature, agriculture, remembrance, community and harmony.
135.text:
Sikkim Chief Minister Prem Singh Tamang on Friday, September 25, highlighted the contribution of the Newar community to the state’s development, saying the Indrajatra festival embodies values of nature, agriculture, remembrance, community and harmony.

Addressing the state-level Indrajatra Celebration 2026 organised by the Sikkim Newar Guthi (SNG), Tamang said members of the Newar community had made significant contributions to Sikkim’s administration, agriculture, trade, mining, culture, arts, sports and social service.

He recalled the contributions of early Newar pioneers, including Laxmidas Pradhan and Chandrabir Pradhan, to administration, agriculture, trade, copper mining and coin production during the early years of Sikkim’s history.

“Indrajatra is not merely a festival but a celebration of nature, agriculture, remembrance, community and harmony,” Tamang said, stressing that the festival carries a message of mutual respect and goodwill.

The chief minister also highlighted the achievements of members of the Newar community in administration, mountaineering, sports, arts and music, saying their contributions had helped bring recognition to Sikkim.

Tamang said the state government was committed to the inclusive development of all communities and had taken steps to provide them greater space to strengthen their institutions and promote their cultural and social interests.

Referring to the Chief Minister’s Education Assistance Scheme, he said students from across Sikkim, including those from the Newar community, had benefited from financial assistance for higher education, medical education and other professional courses.

He stressed the need to ensure that government schemes and development initiatives reach those who need them and reiterated his government’s commitment to the welfare of people across the state.

During the programme, Tamang handed over the land parcha to the Sikkim Newar Guthi for construction of its bhawan and unveiled the logo of the first Sikkim Travel and Tourism Fair 2026.

He also felicitated the recipients of the Newar Ratna Samman 2026 and Bhanji Bhrikuti Samman. Suryavir Tuladhar, Govind Prasad Pradhan and Ganesh Kumar Pradhan received the Newar Ratna Samman, while Suchitna Tamang was conferred the Bhanji Bhrikuti Samman for her contributions and achievements.

The chief minister also released Smarika 2026, the annual publication documenting the community’s activities, achievements and cultural heritage. The publication has been released in both print and digital formats this year.

The Ritual Book and Newar Indrajatra Song were also released during the event.

The fourth day of the state-level celebration featured traditional Newar performances and rituals, including Kumari Nritya, Bajrayogini Nritya, Newari folk dance, Dhimey Dance and Pancha Kumari Nritya, along with musical performances and community offerings.

136.title: ISL comes to Imphal as NorthEast United expand home footprint
136.description: NorthEast United FC will host Sporting Club Delhi in Imphal on November 24, the first Indian Super League match in Manipur at Khuman Lampak Stadium.
136.text:
Indian Super League (ISL) football is finally coming to Manipur.

NorthEast United FC will take on Sporting Club Delhi at the Khuman Lampak Stadium in Imphal on November 24, marking the first ISL match to be staged in the football-mad state.

ADVERTISEMENT

Stay connected Make The News Mill your preferred source See more TNM stories when you search for news on Google. Add TNM on Google

The 7.30 pm fixture, announced on September 26 as part of the first phase of the ISL 2026-27 schedule, is one of the most significant additions to the league’s geographical footprint this season. The fixture list confirms Imphal as a new ISL destination, with NorthEast United designated as the home team.

For Manipur, which has endured prolonged ethnic unrest and violence in recent years, the arrival of the country’s top football league carries significance beyond the 90 minutes on the pitch. Violence and security concerns have continued to affect parts of the state.

ADVERTISEMENT

What has rarely been in question, however, is Manipur’s relationship with football.

Khuman Lampak has already demonstrated what it can offer on a major football night. When the Indian senior men’s national team played in Imphal for the first time during the Tri-Nation International Tournament in March 2023, almost 30,000 spectators packed the stadium for India’s matches. The AIFF described the stands as full well before kick-off for the opener against Myanmar, while another capacity crowd turned up for India’s 2-0 win over Kyrgyz Republic.

The response to the Durand Cup in Imphal has further underlined the appetite for top-level football in the state. The 2026 tournament again included Khuman Lampak among its venues, continuing the city’s growing presence on the national football calendar.

ADVERTISEMENT

Against that backdrop, NorthEast United’s meeting with Sporting Club Delhi has the ingredients for one of the most atmospheric fixtures of the first phase of the ISL season.

From Guwahati to Shillong, and now Imphal

The move also represents another step in NorthEast United’s attempt to live up to its identity as a club representing the entire region rather than one city.

For most of its existence, the Highlanders have played their home matches at the Indira Gandhi Athletic Stadium in Guwahati. The club subsequently adopted Shillong as another home venue, staging ISL matches at the Jawaharlal Nehru Stadium.

In an interaction with The News Mill in February 2025, NorthEast United chief executive officer Mandar Tamhane had explained that the club wanted to take matches to other northeastern states whenever suitable infrastructure was available.

At the time, Tamhane specifically referred to Manipur having hosted the Indian national team, while noting that circumstances in the state made staging an ISL fixture difficult then.

“Wherever the infrastructure allows us to host an ISL game, we will be more than happy to play,” Tamhane had told TheNewsMill.

Less than two years later, Imphal is on the ISL map.

Under the first-phase schedule released on September 26, NorthEast United’s other listed home fixtures are at the Sarusajai Stadium in Guwahati. They include matches against Mohun Bagan Super Giant, Kerala Blasters, Bengaluru FC, FC Goa, Punjab FC and Chennaiyin FC.

Shillong is expected to return to the Highlanders’ home calendar when the remaining fixtures are announced, with matches likely during the later part of the season.

For now, though, November 24 belongs to Imphal — and if Manipur’s recent history of turning up for big football occasions is any indication, Khuman Lampak could be in for a memorable ISL debut.

137.title: IFA Shield — NorthEast United beats Sreenidi to qualify for semifinal; Punjab takes on Calcutta Customs
137.description: Jithin MS scored the opening goal, before Danny Laishram doubled the advantage and Alaaeddine Ajaraie completed the scoring for NorthEast United.
137.text:
NorthEast United FC began its IFA Shield campaign with a commanding 3-0 victory over Sreenidi Deccan FC in a Group A fixture at the Barasat Stadium on Saturday.

Jithin MS scored the opening goal, before Danny Laishram doubled the advantage and Alaaeddine Ajaraie completed the scoring in the second half.

Jithin opened the scoring just seven minutes into the contest, after Asheer and Ajaraie combined to set up Jithin, who made no mistake with a composed finish into the bottom-right corner.

The Highlanders were dealt a blow when Mohammed Arshaf went down injured, forcing an early change in the 24th minute, but Laishram made an immediate impact, doubling the lead after the half-hour mark.

Parthib Gogoi, coming off the bench, set up Ajaraie after the restart as the Moroccan forward netted his 49th goal for the club.

Though Sreenidi continued to search for a breakthrough, the two-time Durand Cup champion proved to be too strong for the Indian Football League side.

The result also saw the Highlanders qualify for the semifinals from the Group.

Punjab FC gears up for IFA Shield clash against Calcutta Customs

On Sunday, the IFA Shield will see Punjab FC take on Calcutta Customs Club in Barasat on Sunday.

The match serves as the first official outing for Punjab’s newly-appointed head coach Pavlos Dermitzakis. The Greek tactician has named a revamped 24-member squad for the tournament.

“We have built a formidable mix of experienced international players, established domestic leaders, and talented young boys from our Roundglass Academy,” Dermitzakis said.

“Calcutta Customs is a resilient side that knows the local conditions very well, but our focus remains on executing our tactical patterns, maintaining our discipline, and starting the group stage with a positive result,” he added.

Calcutta Customs, on the other hand, will start as the underdog after its 1-3 loss against the Indian Super League champion East Bengal FC.

The match will kick off at 2:30 pm.

Published on Sep 26, 2026

138.title: Assam Rifles: India’s Only Paramilitary Force
138.description: The Assam Rifles is one of the most distinctive forces in India’s security architecture — and one of the least understood.Its origins go back to 1835, when it was raised as the Cachar Levy wit
138.text:
The Assam Rifles is one of the most distinctive forces in India’s security architecture — and one of the least understood.

Its origins go back to 1835, when it was raised as the Cachar Levy with just 750 men. Created to protect British interests and settlements in the Northeast, the force went through several transformations — Assam Frontier Police, Assam Military Police and Eastern Bengal and Assam Military Police — before taking its present name in 1917.

Nearly two centuries later, the Assam Rifles remains deeply embedded in the security landscape of the Northeast.

Unlike the Central Armed Police Forces — CRPF, BSF, CISF, ITBP and SSB — the Assam Rifles has a distinctive Army-linked command structure. Its administrative affairs fall under the Ministry of Home Affairs, while its operational command is exercised through the Army. Its senior leadership is drawn from serving Army officers, with the Director General being a serving Lieutenant General.

Watch: Assam Rifles Remains Significant, With Expanded Role On China Border, Besides Traditional Duties

This unusual arrangement has also been the subject of a long-running institutional debate over administrative and operational control.

The force has an extraordinary operational history. It fought in both World Wars, was among the first Indian forces to confront the Chinese offensive in NEFA in 1962, played a major role during the Mizo insurgency, participated in Operation Pawan in Sri Lanka and has undertaken counter-insurgency operations in the Northeast and Jammu & Kashmir.

Its history is also closely linked to some defining moments in independent India. In 1951, Major Bob Khathing led an expedition to Tawang, while in 1959, Assam Rifles personnel escorted the Dalai Lama and his entourage after they crossed into India from Tibet.

Today, the Assam Rifles has another crucial responsibility: guarding India’s 1,643-km-long border with Myanmar. The frontier brings together insurgency, narcotics trafficking, refugee flows, Myanmar’s internal conflict, China’s growing influence and India’s Act East ambitions.

At the same time, the force continues its civic role in remote areas — running schools, providing healthcare and supporting communities.

In this Defence Mantra Classroom, we explore the history, structure, operations and evolving role of the Assam Rifles — a force that has spent nearly two centuries guarding India’s eastern frontier.

139.title: Arunachal Governor, GOC 101 area discuss civil-military coordination, humanitarian assistance and disaster relief preparedness
139.description: During the meeting on Friday, the Governor appreciated the role of 101 Area, headquartered in Shillong, in ensuring combat logistics and operational coordination across the region.
139.text:
Itanagar (Arunachal Pradesh) [India], September 26 (ANI): General Officer Commanding (GOC) 101 Area, Lt Gen Mohit Waghwa, called on Arunachal Pradesh Governor Lt Gen KT Parnaik at Lok Bhavan, Itanagar, and discussed issues related to logistics support, civil-military coordination and humanitarian assistance and disaster relief (HADR) mechanisms in the North-East.

During the meeting on Friday, the Governor appreciated the role of 101 Area, headquartered in Shillong, in ensuring combat logistics and operational coordination across the region.

He lauded the Command’s prompt response during natural disasters, including floods and landslides, where rescue, relief and rehabilitation efforts provided support to affected communities.

Highlighting Arunachal Pradesh’s strategic importance, the Governor stressed the need to further strengthen coordination between the Armed Forces, State Government and civil administration for effective disaster response and public welfare initiatives.

He also suggested improving transit routes, communication networks and administrative infrastructure to support troop movement and border area logistics.

The Governor urged the GOC to strengthen welfare measures for Ex-Servicemen and Veer Naris, with special focus on improving access to the Ex-Servicemen Contributory Health Scheme (ECHS), empanelment of state healthcare institutions and other welfare programmes.

He also highlighted the importance of resettlement and skill development initiatives, educational assistance for children of Ex-Servicemen, pension-related services and reemployment opportunities for veterans.

The Governor suggested organising regular awareness camps, medical outreach programmes in remote areas and closer coordination with the Rajya Sainik Board and Zila Sainik Boards to ensure eligible veterans and their families receive available benefits.

The GOC assured the Governor of the Indian Army’s continued commitment towards maintaining coordination and extending support for the security, development and welfare of the people of Arunachal Pradesh.

Meanwhile, the Governor visited the Armed Forces Goodwill Enclosures at Ziro in Lower Subansiri district and appreciated the efforts of the Indian Army, Indian Air Force and Border Roads Organisation (BRO) in creating awareness among citizens and encouraging youth to join the Armed Forces.

The Governor visited various stalls showcasing defence capabilities, including the ‘Know Your Army’ Stall, Equipment Display Stall, BRO Stall, Indian Air Force Stall, NCC and Sainik School Stall.

He said such initiatives help bridge the gap between the Armed Forces and citizens by providing young people with exposure to opportunities and challenges associated with military service.

The Governor also interacted with visitors and encouraged youth to explore opportunities to serve the nation with dedication and commitment. (ANI)

140.title: AFSPA extended in Manipur, Nagaland and Arunachal Pradesh: What does the law mean? | Explained
140.description: AFSPA extended in parts of Manipur, Nagaland, and Arunachal Pradesh for six months, amid shifting security dynamics and debated power, scope, and governance.
140.text:
The Story So Far : The Union Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) has extended the Armed Forces (Special Powers) Act, 1958 (AFSPA) in parts of Manipur, Nagaland and Arunachal Pradesh for another six months from October 1, 2026.

In Manipur, the entire State has been declared a “disturbed area” under AFSPA, barring the jurisdictions of 13 police stations in five Valley districts: Imphal, Lamphel, City, Singjamei, Patsoi, Wangoi, Porompat, Heingang, Irilbung, Thoubal, Bishnupur, Nambol and Kakching.

The latest order comes against the backdrop of the ethnic conflict that erupted in Manipur on May 3, 2023. Though AFSPA had progressively been withdrawn from several areas of the State before the conflict, MHA began restoring it in some areas after the security situation deteriorated.

In Nagaland, AFSPA will continue in nine districts: Dimapur, Niuland, Chumoukedima, Mon, Kiphire, Noklak, Phek, Peren and Meluri, as well as areas under 21 police stations in five other districts: Kohima, Mokokchung, Longleng, Wokha and Zunheboto.

In Arunachal Pradesh, the Act has been extended in Tirap, Changlang and Longding districts, and in areas under the Namsai, Mahadevpur and Chowkham police stations in Namsai district bordering Assam.

What is AFSPA?

AFSPA was enacted in 1958 to give the armed forces special powers to operate in areas declared “disturbed” because of insurgency or serious internal security problems.

Once an area is notified as disturbed under Section 3 of the Act, security personnel operating there receive powers that ordinary police do not have. The law authorises the armed forces, subject to conditions specified in the Act, to use force, including lethal force, against persons acting in contravention of prohibitory orders; arrest without a warrant; and enter and search premises without a warrant.

It also provides legal protection to personnel acting under the Act. Prosecution, suit or other legal proceedings in respect of anything done or purported to be done under AFSPA require the previous sanction of the Central government.

It is these extraordinary powers and the protection against prosecution without the Centre’s sanction that make AFSPA contentious.

Who can declare an area “disturbed”?

An important feature of AFSPA is that both the Central government and State governments have the power to declare an area disturbed under Section 3. This explains why the geographical application of the law has not always been determined solely by the MHA.

For decades, the Manipur government itself issued the disturbed-area notifications. Though AFSPA had been in operation in the State since 1981, MHA had largely left the periodic renewal of the notification to the State government, which changed after the May 3, 2023 ethnic violence.

The law first came into effect in 1958 to deal with the uprising in the Naga Hills, followed by the insurgency in Assam. It gives unbridled power to the armed forces and the Central Armed Police Forces deployed in “disturbed areas” to kill anyone acting in contravention of law, arrest and search any premises without a warrant and protection from prosecution and legal suits without the Central government’s sanction.

Currently, the Union Home Ministry issues periodic “disturbed area” notification to extend the AFSPA only for Nagaland and Arunachal Pradesh, where it is applicable in the districts of Tirap, Changlang, Longding and areas falling under Namsai and Mahadevpur police stations bordering Assam.

The notification for Assam is issued by the State governments. Tripura revoked the Act in 2015 and Meghalaya was under the AFSPA for 27 years, until it was revoked by the Ministry from April 1, 2018. The Act was implemented in a 20-km area along the border with Assam. Jammu and Kashmir has a separate J&K Armed Forces (Special Powers) Act, 1990.

How did AFSPA gradually shrink in Manipur?

AFSPA’s footprint in Manipur had been contracting before the current ethnic conflict. Its application was withdrawn from the Imphal municipal area in 2004. A much more substantial rollback began in 2022, when the security situation was considered to have improved.

Between April 1, 2022 and April 1, 2023, AFSPA was withdrawn from all police station areas in the Manipur Valley. The State government cited an improved security situation and a greater sense of security among the public.

AFSPA, however, continued in the hill regions, where disturbed-area notifications had been renewed periodically for decades. The trajectory therefore appeared to be towards a gradual reduction in AFSPA-covered territory. The violence beginning in May 2023 reversed that trend.

On November 14, 2024, the MHA reimposed AFSPA in Manipur in the jurisdictions of six police stations spread across five districts: Sekmai and Lamsang in Imphal West, Lamlai in Imphal East, Jiribam in Jiribam district, Moirang in Bishnupur and Leimakhong in Kangpokpi.

These were among the areas from which AFSPA had earlier been withdrawn.

The MHA said the notification was necessary to enable “well-coordinated operations by the security forces” and to contain the activities of insurgent groups.

The move was noteworthy not merely because AFSPA was returning to some places, but also because the notification came from the MHA rather than the Manipur government.

Did the Manipur government agree with MHA?

No. The State government sought a reversal almost immediately.

On November 15, 2024, the Manipur Cabinet under then Chief Minister N. Biren Singh decided to recommend that the Centre review and withdraw the November 14 notification in “public interest”. The State government conveyed the decision to the Union Home Secretary the following day.

The disagreement was unusual because the Centre and the State, both then governed by the BJP, took different positions on whether AFSPA should be restored in those six police station areas.

Political circumstances subsequently changed significantly. President’s Rule was imposed in Manipur on February 13, 2025 and revoked on February 4, 2026.

Why does the latest notification matter?

Before the 2023 violence, the direction of government policy in Manipur had been towards progressively reducing the territory covered by AFSPA. By April 2023, all valley police station areas had been excluded.

The November 2024 notification marked a partial reversal when the Centre restored the law in six police station jurisdictions.

The latest arrangement still exempts 13 police stations in five valley districts, but keeps the rest of the State within the disturbed-area notification. This demonstrates how the security situation following the 2023 ethnic violence interrupted the earlier process of shrinking AFSPA’s geographical footprint.

Why does AFSPA continue in Nagaland and Arunachal Pradesh?

In Nagaland, the continuation of AFSPA has historically been linked to the presence and movement of armed insurgent groups as well as the unresolved Naga political issue.

The Centre has held negotiations with the National Socialist Council of Nagaland (Isak-Muivah), or NSCN-IM, and Naga National Political Groups (NNPGs). In 2022, security officials had indicated that uncertainty over the conclusion of the Naga peace process was one reason AFSPA continued in some areas of Nagaland and neighbouring States.

In Arunachal Pradesh, its application has been concentrated largely in districts affected by insurgent movement and areas adjoining Assam. Tirap, Changlang and Longding have consequently continued under the Act, along with specified police station jurisdictions in Namsai district.

The present system is therefore no longer one in which AFSPA uniformly covers much of the Northeast. Its application has progressively been narrowed to particular States, districts and even individual police station jurisdictions based on periodic security assessments.

Has AFSPA been rolled back elsewhere in the Northeast?

Yes. The geographical reach of AFSPA has considerably declined compared with the situation a few years ago.

Assam provides a significant example. Until March 31, 2022, AFSPA applied across Assam and Nagaland. Beginning April 1 that year, the Centre and State governments substantially reduced the areas designated as disturbed in Assam, Nagaland and Manipur. The Disturbed Areas Notification is in force since 1990 in the whole of Assam.

AFSPA is currently restricted to Tinsukia, Charaideo and Sivasagar districts. The Assam government said security conditions had “significantly improved” over the past three years, but retained the Act in these three districts because ULFA (Independent) remains the State’s only major active militant group and uses routes through Arunachal Pradesh and Nagaland to access camps in Myanmar. The three districts are also considered vulnerable because of their location along the Assam-Nagaland and Assam-Arunachal Pradesh borders.

The earlier reductions coincided with a decline in insurgency-related violence and the surrender or arrest of militants. Security officials also argued that where the deployment of the Army itself had declined, retaining the special statutory powers available under AFSPA had become increasingly difficult to justify.

The Centre had consequently presented the shrinking AFSPA footprint as part of the broader improvement in the Northeast’s security situation.

Also read | Extended exclusion: On AFSPA in Manipur

AFSPA was removed from whole of Tripura by the CPI-M led State Government in 2015.

Manipur is now the important exception to that trajectory. While AFSPA was being progressively withdrawn from the valley until 2023, the ethnic conflict that began that year led to its return to some previously exempted areas and has ensured that most of the State remains covered by the law.

What about Jammu and Kashmir?

Jammu and Kashmir has a separate J&K Armed Forces (Special Powers) Act, 1990.

141.title: One more arrested in Mizoram Army man's killing case
141.description: One more person was arrested in connection with the killing of an Army man in Mizoram’s Kolasib district, taking the total number of people arrested in the case to nine, police said on Friday, September 25.
141.text:
One more person was arrested in connection with the killing of an Army man in Mizoram’s Kolasib district, taking the total number of people arrested in the case to nine, police said on Friday, September 25.

The latest accused, a 31-year-old man from Kawnpui town in Kolasib district, was arrested and subsequently sent to judicial custody, a police officer said.

Army personnel Zakaria Lalhriattluanga, 29, serving with the Assam Regiment and deployed in Jammu and Kashmir, was allegedly beaten to death by a group of youths in Kolasib on September 20 while he was returning to his native village, New Builum.

Police had earlier arrested eight people, including a woman and two minors, in connection with the killing. Six adults were sent to the district jail, while the two minors were handed over to the Juvenile Justice Board.

Meanwhile, Mizoram Home Minister K Sapdanga is scheduled to visit Zakaria’s parents on Saturday to offer condolences and hand over ex-gratia assistance to the bereaved family, officials said.

Chief Minister Lalduhoma had on Thursday condemned the killing, saying the incident had brought disrepute to the state and its people.

Police are continuing their investigation into the circumstances surrounding the Army man’s death.

142.title: AFSPA extended in Manipur for six months, 13 police station areas excluded
142.description: The latest extension follows fresh attacks reported across several districts amid continuing law and order concerns
142.text:
New Delhi, Sept 26: The Centre has extended the Armed Forces (Special Powers) Act (AFSPA) in Manipur for another six months from October 1, keeping most of the state under the “disturbed area” declaration, while excluding areas under 13 police stations in five districts.

The extension was notified by the Ministry of Home Affairs on September 25 following a review of the law and order situation. The notification will remain in force until March 31, 2027, unless withdrawn earlier.

The areas excluded from the AFSPA ambit are under City, Imphal, Lamphel, Singjamei, Patsoi and Wangoi police stations in Imphal West; Heingang, Irilbung and Porompat in Imphal East; Thoubal police station in Thoubal; Bishnupur and Nambol in Bishnupur district; and Kakching police station in Kakching district.

AFSPA empowers armed forces personnel in areas declared “disturbed” to carry out operations, including searches and arrests, under specified provisions of the law.

The law has been in force in Manipur since the early 1980s, though its geographical ambit has been progressively reduced over the years.

In 2004, AFSPA was withdrawn from the Imphal Municipality area, covering seven Assembly constituencies.

In April 2022, the Centre revoked the law from areas under 15 police stations across six districts, while four more police station areas were excluded from the “disturbed area” notification with effect from April 1, 2023.

The latest extension comes amid continuing security concerns and fresh incidents of violence in parts of the state.

On Thursday, four civilians were killed in an attack at Pilong village in Kamjong district, near the India-Myanmar border.

According to officials, unidentified armed persons suspected to be members of a Myanmar-based rebel group entered the village and opened fire on residents. Police and security forces subsequently recovered the bodies.

Two days earlier, a 36-year-old civilian electricity lineman was killed amid heavy firing in and around Lasan and Songpibung villages along the IT Road corridor.

Reports also said several Naga villages along the Noney-Kangpokpi-Senapati belt came under attack, with residents fleeing some areas.

The latest violence has added to security concerns in the state, where armed clashes, attacks and tensions between communities have continued in several hill districts.

143.title: Assam Rifles conducts civic action programmes, outreach across Nagaland
143.description: Assam Rifles conducts civic initiatives, youth outreach, and cleanliness drives across several districts in Nagaland.
143.text:
DIMAPUR — Assam Rifles conducted a series of civic action drives, educational exposure tours, youth training programmes, and community-centric activities across multiple districts in Nagaland.





Youths performing pull-ups on an outdoor bar while others look on during a physical training session in Tuensang.





Kohima: The Kohima Garrison of Assam Rifles is conducting a Seema Darshan Tour for 20 students and two teachers of Government Higher Secondary School, Rusoma village, Kohima district, under Operation Sadbhavana for the academic year 2026-27.





According to an update, during the ongoing tour, the students visited Tenga and Shergaon, where they interacted with senior military leadership and visited an apple and kiwi orchard, Ball of Fire Museum, Tenga Hut, and the local market.

Meluri: Assam Rifles organised 'A day with company commander' on September 25 at Meluri for the students of S Pethuri Montessori School, Meluri. 144.title: Assam Rifles engages youth in Nagaland, Manipur
144.description: Assam Rifles engages youth in Nagaland, Manipur
144.text:
Kohima, Imphal, Sep 27: Assam Rifles under the Spear Corps conducted youth engagement programmes under the initiative “A Day with Company Commander” across Nagaland and Manipur, providing students opportunities to interact with security personnel, explore career options and participate in educational and community activities.

At Meluri and Mon in Nagaland, students attended motivational lectures and career-guidance sessions focused on opportunities to join the Armed Forces. The programmes also included sports activities and tree plantation drives, encouraging participants to adopt healthy lifestyles and contribute to environmental conservation.

The interactions provided students an opportunity to learn about discipline, leadership, teamwork and the values associated with service in the Armed Forces. Career counselling sessions also sought to familiarise young participants with various pathways available to them in the defence services.

In Sangaikot and Khongsang in Manipur, Assam Rifles organised interactive sessions and career counselling programmes for students. An awareness capsule on the constructive use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) was also conducted, highlighting the potential of emerging technology as a tool for education, learning and personal development.

The programmes encouraged students to engage in informed discussions on career choices, technology and their responsibilities towards society. The interactive format enabled participants to ask questions and gain a better understanding of opportunities available beyond conventional career pathways.

The initiative also sought to strengthen interaction between youth and the security forces by creating a platform for dialogue, mentorship and awareness.

Through activities combining motivation, sports, environmental awareness, career guidance and technology education, the “A Day with Company Commander” programme aimed to encourage young people to pursue constructive goals and develop qualities such as discipline, confidence, leadership and social responsibility.

The Assam Rifles said such youth-focused engagements are intended to provide meaningful exposure to students while encouraging them to explore opportunities, develop their skills and contribute positively to their communities.

145.title: BonV Aero Supplies 45 UAVs to Indian Army’s Eastern Command for Tactical Logistics
145.description: Raksha Anirveda is India’s premier defence, aerospace, and security news magazine covering strategic affairs, defence technology, military updates, policy analysis, and global security trends. Stay informed with expert insights and the latest updates in defence and aerospace industry.
145.text:
New Delhi: BonV Aero, a heavy-payload UAV manufacturer from Odisha, has supplied 45 unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) to the Indian Army’s Eastern Command to support tactical missions, including moving critical supplies and other mission-specific payloads. The deployment extends the company’s aerial mobility solutions to support missions across Northeast India’s challenging terrain.

The move comes as the Ministry of Defence recently floated a tender for 2,715 logistics drones. The scale of the request reflects the growing role of UAVs in frontline operations, including moving essential supplies and other mission-critical payloads across challenging terrain.

The delivered UAV systems are purpose-built for multi-role frontline operations, providing a resilient aerial logistics capability to transport critical supplies, operational equipment, and mission-configured payloads and enhancing operational reach in complex environments.

The Eastern Command operates across a diverse geographical area, from forested and riverine stretches to high-altitude Himalayan posts. During the monsoon, flooding and landslides can disrupt road routes, while higher-altitude locations face snow, steep approaches, and rapidly changing weather.

The Indian Army has been seeking drone-based solutions to move essential supplies across inaccessible areas in the Northeast, while also addressing the region’s persistent security challenges. The deployment of 45 BonV Aero UAVs responds directly to this operational need.

“Aerial mobility solutions can act as a force multiplier for the Indian Army, particularly in terrain where surface-based movement has traditionally been the primary means of moving essential supplies. Heavy-payload UAVs can complement existing modes of movement by enabling troops to receive critical supplies and other mission-specific payloads even when terrain, weather or accessibility pose challenges. As these systems become more capable, the focus will be on improving payload capacity, range, reliability, ease of deployment, field-level maintenance and mission adaptability, while ensuring they can be effectively sustained and integrated into frontline operations,” said Satyabrata Satapathy, Co-founder and CEO, BonV Aero.

BonV Aero has previously carried out drone operations and trials for the Army in Tawang, Siliguri, Dimapur, Kargil, Dras, Nyoma, Baramulla, and Kupwara. In addition, the company has trained more than 150 Army personnel on its systems in the Northern Command.

BonV Aero holds a world record for carrying a 30-kg payload to 19,024 feet at Umling La. The operation took place in mountain and glacier terrain, where low oxygen levels, extreme cold, and high-altitude conditions test both flight performance and operational planning. It also reflects the growing role these platforms play in supporting critical supplies and other operational needs in strategically important areas.

146.title: CIJW school conducts seminar on northeast India
146.description:
Counter Insurgency and Jungle Warfare School, Vairengte, conducted a two-day seminar on “Cultural Diplomacy, Ecosystem of Tribals and Indigenous People, Population-Centric Engagement and Way Ahead for Northeast India” on 23-24 September 2026.

The seminar brought together eminent moderators and
146.text:
Counter Insurgency and Jungle Warfare School, Vairengte, conducted a two-day seminar on “Cultural Diplomacy, Ecosystem of Tribals and Indigenous People, Population-Centric Engagement and Way Ahead for Northeast India” on 23-24 September 2026.

The seminar brought together eminent moderators and speakers from NIT Silchar, Assam University, Central University of Jharkhand, Mizoram University, North-Eastern Hill University, Tripura University, the Indian Institute of Public Administration, and DIPR, DRDO, along with army officers, academicians, and students. The three thematic sessions brought academic research, professional experience and local understanding onto a common platform.

The first thematic session, “Cultural Diplomacy & Ecosystem of Tribals and Indigenous People,” explored the cultural strengths of Northeast India and their potential for strengthening people-to-people linkages. The second thematic session, “Population-Centric Engagement,” placed trust at the centre of meaningful engagement with local populations.

The final thematic session, “Economic & Technological Pathways & Way Ahead,” focused on future development opportunities for the region. Participants analysed extensive comparative economic data and offered suggestions the strengthen economic development in Northeast India. The technological dimension highlighted existing Government technology initiatives while also proposing new technology-enabled solutions to improve governance, accessibility, service delivery, and development outcomes.

An interesting progression of ideas also emerged through the two days. The discourse began with the 3 Cs — Connectivity, Culture and Community, emphasising that regional engagement must go beyond physical connectivity alone. As the discussion widened towards cross-border linkages and cooperation, the thought expanded to the 5 Cs — Culture, Community, Connectivity, Cooperation and Confidence.

In his closing remarks, Maj Gen Kulvir Singh, SM, PhD, Commandant, CIJW School, carried this progression further into a comprehensive 7 Cs framework - Culture, Community, Connectivity, Capacity, Commerce, Confidence and Convergence. He also underscored inclusive growth and meaningful participation of women as essential elements in shaping the way ahead for Northeast India.

This 3-5-7 progression captured the broad journey of the seminar-from cultural understanding and community engagement, through cooperation and confidence, towards capacity building, economic opportunity and convergence of efforts.

The seminar strengthened Army-academia interaction and generated practical perspectives towards an inclusive, people-centric and progressive future for Northeast India.

147.title: From mountain guns to missiles and drones: How India's artillery evolved over nearly 200 years
147.description: In the wee hours of May 7, 2025, the stillness and silence of the night was broken by the big guns of the Indian artillery.
147.text:
A Bofors gun of the artillery firing during an exercise in the North East. (Image credit: Indian Army)

From Panipat to Mysorean rockets: India's long artillery tradition

The modern Indian Artillery

The growing importance of artillery

Different types of sensors will make the artillery the dominant arm in the future.

Artillery in the future will encompass a large portion of the battlefield. There won't be a battle without artillery. Due to the nature of the arm it will be involved in long range kinetic operations and choke point operations in all types of terrain. This will have great value as this capability will have huge deterrent capability. But to fully exploit this, we need ground, air and space based sensors. There is a need to think of artillery differently, to make use of upcoming capabilities, the current way of thinking will not let us take full advantage of these systems. Lt Gen PR Shankar (retired), Professor, Aerospace Dept IIT Madras and former DG Artillery

The Regiment of artillery has grown in quantity and quality over the years, with more changes to come.

The eyes behind the guns: ISR, drones and the kill chain

Drones, rockets, artillery and missiles are changing the way the gunners employ their skills.

What India now needs its artillery to do

In the wee hours of May 7, 2025, the stillness and silence of the night was broken by the big guns of the Indian artillery. Although the attacks on the terror nerve centres at Muridke and Bahawalpur stole the headlines, the Army had struck seven more targets across both the Line of Control and the international border.These targets were hit by precision fire from artillery guns and loitering munitions. The message was clear: there was no safe space on the other side of the border.The pinpoint dropping of munitions on these terror targets was the latest feat in a long and storied history of the artillery arm, which now has nearly 200 years of service under its belt.The importance of long-range firepower in a non-contact but kinetic conflict has grown in the last few years, as demonstrated first in Ukraine and then reiterated by Iran. The Americans, too, have shown their dependence on long-range vectors such as the Tomahawk cruise missile and the PrSM to degrade adversarial air defences before sending in aircraft for stand-in attacks.India, which is unlikely to be inducting stealth aircraft in the near future, is more likely to depend on stand-off weapons in the initial phases of a conflict, as was demonstrated during Operation Sindoor. Artilleryâs unique capability to âstrike deep and strike hardâ is therefore even more important for the country.The Regiment of Artillery has, from its first use in the sub-continent during the mid-14th century Bahmani-Vijayanagar War, only grown in significance. In the Battle of Panipat in 1526, artillery was decisively used to defeat the much larger Delhi Sultanate army of Ibrahim Lodhi, thus laying the foundation of the Mughal Empire. Though the artillery arm of the Marathas was weaker than many of their contemporaries, Balaji Baji Rao organised the arm on professional lines and Madhavji Sindhia established a fairly efficient gun manufacturing foundry under the supervision of European gun makers.The Indian artillery tradition has left another mark halfway around the world. The American national anthem also gives an ode to the Indian artillery tradition, with the lines âand the rocketsâ red glare, the bombs bursting in air, gave proof through the night that our flag was still thereâ. The red glare of the rockets that features prominently in the US national anthem came from rockets fired by the British at Fort McHenry during the War of 1812. But the British had themselves been at the receiving end of Mysorean rockets and, after the defeat of Tipu Sultan, adapted the technology into what came to be known as the Congreve rocket.The modern Regiment of Artillery traces its origins to September 28, 1827, when the British East India Company raised 5 (Bombay) Mountain Battery, originally the 8th Company of the Golandaz Battalion, Bombay Foot Artillery. It was the first unit of what would eventually become the Regiment and the first to be manned by native Indian soldiers. Specialising in mountain warfare, it set the template for the versatile artillery units the Army fields today.By the time of Independence, Indian Artillery had grown into a multi-branch arm, comprising Field, Medium, Air Defence, Counter Bombardment, Coastal, Air Observation Post and Survey units. Partition then split the Royal Indian Artillery, with India retaining eighteen and a half regiments while Pakistan received the remaining nine and a half.The Regiment has since fought in all the major conflicts the nation has fought in. In 1947-48, its guns helped hold key positions in the high-altitude terrain of Kashmir. In 1962, despite being outgunned and ill-prepared, artillery units inflicted considerable damage on the enemy. In 1965, its firepower proved decisive against Pakistani armour. In 1971, it provided overwhelming fire support in both the Eastern and Western theatres. During Kargil in 1999, artillery pounded enemy positions along the ridges, aiding the recapture of Tiger Hill and Tololing, with the Bofors guns earning particular praise for their accuracy.The vast majority of artillery regiments are equipped with the indigenous 105 mm Indian Field Gun or the Light Field Gun, while Pinaka, Dhanush and, in the future, the Advanced Towed Artillery Gun System (ATAGS) will increase the indigenous mix of equipment. The arm also has domestically assembled K9 Vajra guns, while the Russian-origin M-46 130mm artillery gun is also being up-gunned to 155mm domestically.Since then, the Regiment of Artillery has grown by leaps and bounds in numbers and capability. The arm is now the second-largest arm of the Army, following the infantry and followed by the mechanised component. In terms of capability, the arm has grown from initially operating guns such as the 3.7-inch mountain gun and the 25-pounder to the 5.5-inch medium artillery gun.Now, the artillery is in the midst of a modernisation drive known as the Field Artillery Rationalisation Plan, which seeks to bring the gun regiments of the artillery to a common calibre of 155mm. This is the same bore as that of the now-famous Bofors gun.The Regiment of Artillery is also extending its reach with rocket systems such as the Pinaka, which is soon expected to reach an operational range of 120 km. The arm also demonstrated the Suryastra rocket system during this yearâs Republic Day parade. This weapon system has a range of up to 300 kilometres.Apart from these battlefield weapons, the arm is also the custodian of the countryâs tactical and strategic weapons. These range from the BrahMos missile that proved its effectiveness during Operation Sindoor to other weapons, including the Agni and Prithvi series of missiles. Once weapons such as the Long Range Cruise Missile (LRCM), Shaurya and Pralay are inducted, they will also equip the regiment. This means that in any future conflict, artillery will have a central role to play in any shooting conflict.Surveillance and Target Acquisition (SATA) regiments of artillery, which are tasked with monitoring the adversaryâs dispositions, are being armed with Loitering Munitions (LM), thus giving the eyes and ears of the arm a precise manner of punching through the enemyâs defences in a more timely and effective manner. Artillery regiments are expected to deploy an increasing number of drones to keep a tab on enemy movements. Besides existing systems such as electro-optics, weapon locating radars and drones, the arm also requires a constellation of low earth orbit satellites to keep persistent eyes on target.Today, the force rests on two pillars: firepower and Intelligence, Surveillance & Reconnaissance (ISR). Firepower in contemporary warfare is often described through the acronym DRAM, standing for drones, rockets, artillery and missiles. The second pillar, ISR, covers intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance. Without advanced sensors, fast communication and robust networking, firepower is effectively blind.An effective kill chain depends on the seamless pairing of sensor and shooter through secure networks, and the age-old sequence of seeing, acquiring and hitting a target remains a fundamental requirement. Meeting it means integrating space links, electronic warfare capabilities and persistent UAV surveillance so that long-range vectors can strike with precision.Artillery is expected to deliver on five broad requirements. The first is conventional deterrence, the promise of overwhelming precision fire that discourages an adversary from embarking on a misadventure. The second is the ability to strike deep, using long-range vectors, both current and futuristic.The third concerns the contact battle. Rocket forces in several other countries operate in silos that do not lend themselves to battlefield synergy, whereas India needs a force that can reinforce the firepower available to frontline troops and provide additional punch from battalion to corps commanders. The fourth requirement is manoeuvre.In seemingly static battlefields, the force must enable manoeuvre or generate what is termed manoeuvre by fire, restoring mobility to a fight that has stalled, as seen in Ukraine. This also includes the idea of horizontal escalation, as witnessed in Iran, where strategic goals can be pursued without direct troop engagement.

148.title: Assam Rifles Organises Medical Camp in Tripura, Providing Healthcare to Over 350 Villagers
148.description: In a commendable initiative aimed at improving healthcare in rural areas, personnel from the Assam Rifles, part of the Indian Army’s Spear Corps, hosted a
148.text:
In a commendable initiative aimed at improving healthcare in rural areas, personnel from the Assam Rifles, part of the Indian Army’s Spear Corps, hosted a medical camp in Kanchanbari, Tripura. This event successfully catered to the health needs of over 350 villagers from the locality, underscoring the ongoing commitment of the Assam Rifles to support remote communities in Northeast India, where access to regular medical facilities is often scarce.

The medical camp offered extensive healthcare services, including comprehensive medical check-ups and immediate healthcare assistance. Trained medical personnel engaged with local residents, providing them with essential health services that addressed both urgent healthcare needs and fostered an increased awareness of personal health and wellness.

The turnout at the camp highlighted the crucial role of outreach-based healthcare initiatives. Many of the villagers, who lack easy access to major medical centres, significantly benefited from the services provided, illustrating the profound impact such initiatives can have on improving community health standards.

Assam Rifles is known for its civic-action and community outreach efforts alongside its operational duties in the Northeast. These initiatives are not limited to medical camps; they encompass various forms of assistance to local communities and other welfare activities aimed at enhancing quality of life in the region.

The successful execution of the Kanchanbari medical camp exemplifies the Assam Rifles’ dedication to fostering stronger connections with local communities. These efforts not only contribute to enhancing rural healthcare but also play a vital role in uplifting community welfare in Tripura, positively impacting the lives of residents in remote areas.

150.title: Three Agniveers missing in Arunachal’s Dibang floods declared dead after DNA tests
150.description: Cloudburst triggered landslides and flash floods, sweeping away seven Army personnel from camp on August 14
150.text:
New Delhi, Sep 27: Three Indian Army Agniveers who went missing during floods in Arunachal Pradesh’s Dibang Valley on August 14 have been declared dead after their identities were confirmed through DNA testing.

According to the Army, Agniveers Aditya Kumar, Kundan Kumar and Vinod Yadav were deployed in the rugged Dibang region when they went missing after a cloudburst triggered landslides and flash floods.

Eastern Army Commander Lt General V.M.B. Krishnan and all ranks of the Army paid tribute to the three soldiers for their service and expressed condolences to their bereaved families.

The Army said the three Agniveers made the supreme sacrifice while performing their duties and affirmed that it stood firmly with their families during the hour of grief.

The identities of the soldiers were established through DNA testing of mortal remains recovered several days after they went missing.

The remains were subsequently handed over to their families, while urns containing their ashes reached their respective native villages on Saturday.

Aditya Kumar, a native of Bihar’s Vaishali, was cremated in Arunachal Pradesh with full military honours, after which his ashes were taken to his ancestral village.

Villagers in his native place organised a Tiranga Yatra to pay their final respects, with residents gathering along the procession route to bid farewell to the soldier.

Vinod Yadav, a native of Uttar Pradesh’s Auraiya, and Kundan Kumar, from Bihar, also went missing in the August 14 floods in Dibang Valley.

Their families endured a prolonged period of uncertainty until DNA testing confirmed their identities and the remains were handed over, according to the Army.

The flash flood hit the Pasu Pani Army Camp of the 5th Grenadier, washing away two shelters and sweeping away seven Army personnel, according to officials.

Two were rescued, while five, including the three Agniveers, were reported missing.

IANS

151.title: Assam Rifles conducts Seema Darshan tour, cleanliness drive in Kiphire

151.text:
Deputy Inspector General of Assam Rifles (North) waving a chequered flag to welcome a tour bus at Kohima Garrison on Monday.





DIMAPUR — Assam Rifles conducted an educational border tour for students from Rusoma and a cleanliness drive in Kiphire.





According to a defence release, Kohima Garrison of Assam Rifles conducted the flag-in ceremony of the Seema Darshan tour organised for 20 students and two teachers of Government Higher Secondary School, Rusoma village, Kohima district, under Operation Sadbhavana for the academic year 2026-27.





The tour, conducted from September 19 to the 28th, covered Kohima, Guwahati, Tenga, Tawang, Tezpur, and Dimapur, providing the students an opportunity to visit places of national, historical, and educational significance and gain first-hand exposure to the life and functioning of the armed forces.





During the tour, the students visited Tenga, Tawang, and Guwahati, where they interacted with the General Officer Commanding of 5 Mountain Division, visited the apple and kiwi orchards at Shergaon, Ball of Fire Museum, Tenga Hut and Sajini, Jaswant Museum, Tawang War Memorial, Bumla Pass, Sangetsar Tso, and Tawang Monastery.

153.title: BonV Aero Supplies 45 Logistics UAVs to Eastern Command
153.description: Odisha-based BonV Aero supplied 45 heavy-payload Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) to the Indian Army’s Eastern Command on 28 September 2026. The UAVs are meant for tactica
153.text:
Odisha-based BonV Aero supplied 45 heavy-payload Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) to the Indian Army’s Eastern Command on 28 September 2026. The UAVs are meant for tactical logistics and mission-specific operations in Northeast India, where terrain, weather, and limited road access affect surface movement.

Logistics UAVs in Military Supply Chains

Logistics UAVs are unmanned aircraft used to carry supplies, equipment, and mission payloads to operational locations. In military use, they support transport in high-altitude posts, forested areas, riverine belts, and regions affected by landslides or floods.

Heavy-payload UAVs are designed to carry larger loads than standard surveillance drones.

Military logistics drones are used for delivery of rations, ammunition, medical supplies, and spare parts.

High-altitude operations require drones with stable flight systems, stronger batteries, and weather resistance.

Eastern Command and Northeast Terrain

The Indian Army’s Eastern Command is responsible for operational areas in eastern India and parts of the Himalayan frontier. Northeast India includes difficult terrain, dense forests, river systems, and mountain routes where road connectivity can be disrupted by monsoon floods and landslides.

High-altitude Himalayan posts often face low temperatures, thin air, and severe weather conditions. These factors make aerial logistics useful for time-sensitive supply movement in remote military locations.

BonV Aero and Defence Drone Development

BonV Aero has conducted drone operations and trials for the Army at Tawang, Siliguri, Dimapur, Kargil, Dras, Nyoma, Baramulla, and Kupwara. The company has also trained more than 150 Army personnel on its systems within the Northern Command.

The company is developing an ultra-heavy payload, high-altitude drone capable of carrying over 100 kilograms to altitudes above 10,000 feet and distances exceeding 100 kilometres. Such specifications place the platform in the military logistics drone segment.

Important Facts for Exams Unmanned Aerial Vehicles are also called drones and are used in surveillance, logistics, and combat support roles.

The Indian Army has separate operational commands, including Eastern Command and Northern Command.

Tawang, Kargil, Dras, Nyoma, Baramulla, and Kupwara are important military locations in high-altitude border regions.

The Ministry of Defence issued a tender for 2,715 logistics drones, which is linked to wider military modernisation.

Defence Procurement and Future Use

The Ministry of Defence recently issued a tender for 2,715 logistics drones. BonV Aero’s supply forms part of the wider use of aerial mobility systems in military logistics across mountainous regions of India.

154.title: Indian Army's Spear Corps holds cleanliness, environmental awareness drive in Agartala
154.description: The Indian Army's Spear Corps organised an educational and awareness drive for troops stationed in Agartala on September 29 as part of the nationwide Swachh Bharat Campaign, focusing on cleanliness, environmental sustainability and operational health.
154.text:
The Indian Army's Spear Corps organised an educational and awareness drive for troops stationed in Agartala on September 29 as part of the nationwide Swachh Bharat Campaign, focusing on cleanliness, environmental sustainability and operational health.

The day-long programme aimed to reinforce awareness about personal hygiene, sanitation and environmental conservation among service personnel, while promoting sustainable practices in daily military routines and garrison management.

The programme began with a keynote address on the vision and significance of ‘Swachhata Hi Seva 2026’. The address highlighted cleanliness as an important aspect of military discipline, national responsibility and operational efficiency.

Interactive sessions were also held on environmental conservation, with troops encouraged to adopt sustainable habits and understand the impact of individual actions on the surrounding environment.

Personnel were advised to adopt energy-efficient practices, minimise wastage of resources and contribute towards the preservation of local ecosystems.

Focus on health and sanitation

A clinical awareness session was conducted by an Army Medical Officer, focusing on personal hygiene, sanitation and cleanliness as key components of maintaining troop health and operational readiness.

The soldiers were also briefed on modern waste management practices based on the principles of Reduce, Reuse, Recycle and Recharge.

Particular emphasis was placed on reducing plastic waste, recycling organic material and replenishing groundwater through rainwater harvesting systems at military stations.

An Army official said cleanliness and environmental responsibility contribute to troop morale, health and operational preparedness.

“Cleanliness and environmental responsibility are force multipliers that directly contribute to troop morale, health and operational readiness,” the official said.

The official added that through initiatives under the Swachh Bharat Campaign, the Spear Corps remains committed to promoting environmental conservation and maintaining high standards of sanitation across its garrisons.

The Spear Corps is responsible for maintaining operational readiness and security along the northeastern frontier. Besides its operational duties, the formation has also been involved in disaster relief, community development, nation-building initiatives and environmental protection activities across the region.

155.title: Not Bali, This Is India! Hidden Resort In Northeast Goes Viral For Riverside Dining & Tropical Vibes
155.description: This hidden resort in Arunachal Pradesh is going viral for its Bali-like vibes, wooden cottages and a scenic riverside setting.
155.text:
Dreaming of a holiday in Bali or the Maldives but finding it too expensive? What if we told you that you could get the same vibes at TungTao Resort, which is hidden right inside Northeast India? This beautiful resort in Arunachal Pradesh is going viral on social media for its triangular wooden cottages, bamboo shacks and for looking like an exotic beachy destination. Here’s everything you need to know.

Plan A Holiday In Arunachal Pradesh’s TungTao Resort

You don’t need a passport to experience this paradise.😍 This is Tungtao Resort in Namsai, Arunachal Pradesh. Imagine dining with your feet dipped in crystal-clear stream water, surrounded by nature. pic.twitter.com/6vO3GDDunD — Vertigo_Warrior (@VertigoWarrior) September 28, 2026



An X user, @VertigoWarrior, recently posted a video from inside the TungTao Resort in Namsai, Arunachal Pradesh. The small clip showing small cottages and relaxed vibes instantly grabbed the attention of travellers, who wanted to know more about this destination in Northeast India.

The resort gives you tropical, luxury vacation vibes just like Bali or the Maldives, and travellers love it for a few simple reasons. The place features triangular wooden cottages to relax in, bamboo shacks and even a riverside restaurant called The Fisherman’s Deck. The wooden pathways on the river and the cottages with thatched roofs make it look like an exotic and luxurious destination.

Also Read: Indian Army Thinks Beyond Limits, Turns Old Bridge Into Café In Arunachal Pradesh

Resort Offers Villas And Bamboo Cottages

According to the official website of TungTao Resort, “Tung” means deep, while “Tao” means tortoise. Many years back, there was a time when the deep water here was home to huge tortoises and giant mahseers, and it is believed that it continues to be so to this day, but the sightings have become very rare.

At this resort, you can book a TungTao Villa, which is a flying hut above the river with private river access and a special bonfire area. Or you can even opt to stay in a Bamboo Cottage, which comes with a private balcony. The resort also offers framed cottages and standard cottages for people looking for budget stays at the resort.

The place definitely lets you experience a fancy island-style holiday without spending money on expensive international flights. Many people call it “Bali of India”, making it a popular choice for friend groups and couples looking for a quick scenic escape. A room here starts at ₹4,000 per night and can go up to ₹10,800.

So, bookmark this resort for your next holiday!
