198.title: Indian Army’s Spear Corps, APS students observe 'Swachhata Hi Seva' drive at Agartala Military Station
198.description: In line with the nationwide 'Swachhata Hi Seva' campaign, troops of the Indian Army’s Spear Corps, in collaboration with students of Army Public School (APS) Agartala, organised a multi-day series of educational, creative, and community outreach drives from September 29 to October 2 at the Agartala Military Station.
198.text:
Agartala (Tripura) [India], October 3 (ANI): In line with the nationwide 'Swachhata Hi Seva' campaign, troops of the Indian Army’s Spear Corps, in collaboration with students of Army Public School (APS) Agartala, organised a multi-day series of educational, creative, and community outreach drives from September 29 to October 2 at the Agartala Military Station.

The campaign aimed to instil deep environmental consciousness, personal hygiene, and active civic responsibility among young students and military personnel alike.

The four-day initiative culminated on October 2 with a massive outdoor cleanliness drive at the iconic Albert Ekka War Memorial, paying tribute to the nation's fallen heroes through community service, alongside a station-wide Shramdaan (voluntary cleanliness drive) undertaken by Spear Corps volunteers across the garrison.

To foster sustainable habits from an early age, APS Agartala conducted a series of competitions across various grade levels. These included banner- and poster-making activities focused on the 'Swachh Bharat Campaign', an essay writing competition on public health and hygiene solutions, and a drawing contest themed 'Clean, Green & Sustainable Station', where students showcased creative blueprints for eco-friendly military stations.

Simultaneously, Army personnel participated in an extensive cleanliness drive across the cantonment. Troops cleared waste, maintained green belts, beautified public transit corridors, and promoted eco-friendly waste disposal mechanisms throughout the station's residential and operational lines.

"Inculcating environmental responsibility and civic pride in our youth is as vital as maintaining operational readiness. The active involvement of our students at APS Agartala alongside the dedicated Shramdaan by our troops reflects the true spirit of Swachhata Hi Seva—turning civic duty into a shared, lifelong commitment," said a defence spokesperson.

The Spear Corps of the Indian Army, tasked with defending India's borders and maintaining security in the North-East, routinely spearheads ecological preservation, humanitarian relief, and civic welfare initiatives alongside its core operational responsibilities. (ANI)

Organised by the 13 Tripura Battalion NCC under the aegis of the NCC Directorate, North […]
201.text:
Agartala, Oct 2: A 10-day camp bringing together NCC cadets from 17 states began in Tripura on Friday, with Governor Indra Sena Reddy Nallu inaugurating the Bir Bikram Ekta Camp-2026 at the Tripura Institute of Technology (TIT) campus in Narsingarh.

Organised by the 13 Tripura Battalion NCC under the aegis of the NCC Directorate, North Eastern Region, the camp is aimed at promoting cultural exchange and greater understanding among young cadets from different parts of the country.

Addressing the inaugural ceremony, Governor Nallu said the NCC helps instil discipline and patriotism among young people. He said the participation of cadets from 17 states in Tripura was a matter of pride.

The Governor said the camp would allow cadets to showcase the traditions and culture of their respective states while experiencing the heritage and diversity of Tripura and the Northeast.

Cadets from states including Uttar Pradesh and Haryana said they were excited to present their own cultural traditions and learn about the folk culture and way of life of the Northeast.

The inaugural ceremony was attended by Brigadier Nishant Chandel, Commander of 21 Sector Assam Rifles, along with senior officials from the armed forces and the NCC Directorate.

The opening day featured cultural performances, documentary screenings and interactive activities. Governor Nallu also interacted with the cadets over tea and joined them for a group photograph.

The 10-day camp will provide the participating cadets with opportunities for cultural exchange, shared activities and exposure to the diverse traditions of the Northeast.

202.title: From Guwahati to Delhi: How Moharana Choudhury Put Assam’s Environmental Work on a National Stage
202.description: Assam Environmentalist Moharana Choudhury Selected among Top Four Nominees for Times Now Amazing Indians Awards 2026 on 30 September 2026, held at The Taj Palace, New Delhi. Moharana Choudhury, Re…
202.text:
Assam Environmentalist Moharana Choudhury Selected among Top Four Nominees for Times Now Amazing Indians Awards 2026 on 30 September 2026, held at The Taj Palace, New Delhi. Moharana Choudhury, Research Coordinator, Environmental Research and Management Division, Voice of Environment (VoE), Guwahati, has been selected among the Top Four nominees in the Environment & Sustainability category of the prestigious Times Now Amazing Indians Awards 2026.

The recognition places Choudhury among four distinguished nominees featured in the awards platform’s official “Nominees 2026 – Environment & Sustainability” announcement. The event was held in New Delhi on September 30, 2026.

The 2026 Grand Jury of the Times Now Amazing Indians Awards includes: Justice Dhananjaya Y. Chandrachud – Former Chief Justice of India; General Upendra Dwivedi, PVSM, AVSM (Retd.) – Former Chief of the Army Staff, Indian Army. Naina Lal Kidwai – Chairman, Rothschild India; Founder, India Sanitation Coalition; Former Chairman, HSBC India; Prasoon Joshi – Chairperson, Prasar Bharati; Amitabh Kant – Former G20 Sherpa and former CEO, NITI Aayog; Khushboo Sundar – Actor and Producer. Dr Deepa Malik – Padma Shri and Khel Ratna Awardee; India’s first woman Paralympic medallist. A significant recognition for Assam and Northeast India, Choudhury’s selection represents notable national-level recognition of environmental research, sustainability initiatives and community-oriented environmental work emerging from Assam and Northeast India. With more than 14 years of experience in environmental research and management.

Choudhury has worked across waste management, wastewater and water pollution, climate change, disaster resilience, environmental awareness, and community engagement. Through his association with Voice of Environment , he has contributed to environmental campaigns and initiatives involving schools, communities, heritage and iconic sites, plastic and waste management, environmental education and sustainability. From environmental research to community action, Choudhury’s professional work combines scientific research with field-level environmental intervention.

His areas of engagement include sustainable waste management, wastewater management, climate resilience and awareness-building among communities and educational institutions.

His environmental initiatives include campaigns focused on plastic and thermocol reduction, cleanliness and ecological sustainability at key public and heritage sites, environmental education in schools, community awareness, and disaster-response activities. Being featured among the top four nominees in the Environment & Sustainability category of the Times Now Amazing Indians Awards 2026 has provided a national platform to highlight environmental work from Assam. Although Choudhury was not selected as the final category award winner, his inclusion among the Top Four nominees is being viewed as an important milestone for research and the environmental work being undertaken from the Northeast. Speaking about the recognition, Choudhury said: “Being selected among the Top Four nominees in the Environment & Sustainability category of the Times Now Amazing Indians Awards is a deeply encouraging moment for our entire team and the organisation. More importantly, I see this recognition as an opportunity to bring greater national attention to the environmental challenges and community-led solutions emerging from Assam and Northeast India. I am grateful to each and every one who has supported my research, field activities and environmental initiatives over more than a decade.”

Recognition beyond an individual

The nomination also highlights the contribution of environmental researchers, and civil-society groups working on sustainability issues at the regional level.

For Choudhury, the recognition is an encouragement to continue working at the intersection of environmental research, and climate resilience together.

The Times Now Amazing Indians Awards 2026, presented by Times Network, brought together nominees from different fields and provided a national platform to recognise individuals making contributions in their respective areas.

203.title: Assam Rifles seize heroin worth over Rs 5 crore in Mizoram
203.description: The Assam Rifles seized 2,537.72 grams of Heroin No. 4, valued at approximately Rs 5.07 crore, during an intelligence-based operation in Zote area of Mizoram’s Champhai district on October 2.
203.text:
The Assam Rifles seized 2,537.72 grams of Heroin No. 4, valued at approximately Rs 5.07 crore, during an intelligence-based operation in Zote area of Mizoram’s Champhai district on October 2.

Acting on specific intelligence inputs regarding the transportation of narcotics, Assam Rifles personnel launched the operation and intercepted two suspected individuals in the area.

A search led to the recovery of 2,537.72 grams of suspected Heroin No. 4. The consignment was valued at approximately Rs 5,07,54,400 according to the prevailing market rate.

The two apprehended individuals were identified as Myanmar nationals.

The seized narcotics and the two suspects were subsequently handed over to the Excise and Narcotics Department, Champhai, for further investigation and legal proceedings.

The seizure comes amid continued efforts by the Assam Rifles and civil agencies to curb narcotics smuggling along Mizoram’s border with Myanmar. Recent operations in and around Zote have also resulted in the seizure of heroin consignments and arrests.

205.title: After Deadly Pangsau Attack, Another Militant Ambush Plot Foiled in Arunachal
205.description: In a major breakthrough, Assam Rifles, in coordination with other security forces, launched an extensive search operation in the border belt
205.text:
After Deadly Pangsau Attack, Another Militant Ambush Plot Foiled in Arunachal

First Published: 2nd October, 2026 12:17 IST

In a major breakthrough, Assam Rifles, in coordination with other security forces, launched an extensive search operation in the border belt

Written By Northeast Live Digital Desk SHARE IT NOW







Security forces have foiled another major ambush plot by militants in Arunachal Pradesh’s Changlang district, within just 48 hours of the deadly Pangsau Pass attack that left an Assam Rifles Havildar martyred and four personnel injured.

In a major breakthrough, Assam Rifles, in coordination with other security forces, launched an extensive search operation in the border belt and arrested two suspected ULFA-I cadres.

The arrested cadres have been identified as Sahadev Rai alias Bappi Asom and Siraj Asom alias Siraju Alam.

Security forces also recovered an AK-series rifle, an improvised explosive device and a large cache of arms and ammunition during the operation.

According to security inputs, a 20-member group comprising cadres of ULFA-I and NSCN (K-YA) was allegedly preparing to ambush security forces in the area.

The operation comes just two days after a patrol team of the 21 Assam Rifles came under attack near Nampong Nallah, close to Pangsau Pass along the India-Myanmar border, on September 29.

The ambush claimed the life of 42-year-old Havildar Jankhokai Kuki, while four other personnel sustained injuries. The firing was reported at around 6 am.

The NSCN (K-YA) faction reportedly claimed responsibility for the September 29 attack.

Following the ambush, security forces have intensified operations across the strategically sensitive Tirap-Changlang-Longding belt, with increased surveillance and deployment along the India-Myanmar border.

The latest operation underscores the heightened security alert in the region, where dense forest terrain and proximity to insurgent bases across the Myanmar border have historically facilitated militant movement.

208.title: Weekly Defence Dispatch: India readies the Chicken's Neck for a war that opens with missiles, Pakistan's pr...
208.description: As India buries ammunition and command bunkers beneath its most vulnerable 22 km and a slain LeT gunman's Pakistan Army record surfaces, while France studies Sindoor, Firstpost tracks the week's key defence developments
208.text:
As India buries ammunition and command bunkers beneath its most vulnerable 22 km and a slain LeT gunman's Pakistan Army record surfaces, while France studies Sindoor, Firstpost tracks the week's key defence developments

From Chokepoint to Fortress: India Rewrites the Defence of Its Northeast

This image has been generated using AI and is for representational purposes only.

The Army is planning to put much of its ammunition and command setup in the Siliguri Corridor below ground. As reported by News18, the plan includes 12 underground ammunition stores for Army air defence units and underground storage for ammunition of the Smerch, the Russian-made long-range rocket system the Army uses. Twenty-one surface firing positions for the rockets will also be built. Separately, five underground command centres, six communication centres and 12 bomb shelters are on the list. Army Headquarters also plans to set up new military stations in the corridor.

Other ministries are working on the transport side. The Railways is building an underground rail tunnel and doubling the NJP-Siliguri and Thakurganj-Siliguri lines. The road ministry is building a six-lane Gorakhpur-Siliguri expressway, a ring road around Siliguri, and a new six-lane bridge over the Teesta so traffic no longer relies only on the old Coronation Bridge. NH-10 between Sevoke and Rangpo in Sikkim will be upgraded for heavy military vehicles, and three roads will be upgraded to connect NH-17 and NH-27. The SSB's road along the Nepal border is almost finished, and a road along the Bhutan border has been proposed.

Advertisement

The corridor: The corridor is about 22 km wide at its narrowest point. It has Nepal on one side, Bangladesh on the other, and Bhutan to the north. China's Chumbi Valley lies beyond Bhutan, where Indian and Chinese troops faced each other at Doklam in 2017. The Northeast's road and rail links to the rest of the country almost all pass through this strip.

Why the Army wants it underground: Ammunition dumps, headquarters and bridges are fixed targets that an enemy can map ahead of time. In a strip this narrow, there isn't much room to spread them out. China has added missile launchers along the LAC over the past year, and in any conflict, these sites in the corridor would likely be among the first targets.

Storing air defence ammunition underground means the units protecting the corridor can keep firing after an initial strike. Command and communication centres underground help officers stay in touch with troops if the area is bombed or jammed. The Smerch positions enable the Army to strike targets far beyond the corridor without bringing rockets from further inland. These additions complement what is already deployed in the area, including S-400 batteries, BrahMos units and Rafales at Hasimara.

More routes: The road and rail projects tackle a different issue. At present, damage to a bridge or a key stretch of highway can slow traffic to the Northeast for days. Once the new expressway, ring road, connecting roads and rail tunnel are operational, supplies will have several ways through. The Kaladan project in Myanmar will provide another route into the region from outside the corridor.

Advertisement

Bangladesh: Bangladesh is also part of the background. A Chinese company has been reported to be reviving the old airfield at Lalmonirhat, close to the corridor. India has generally not regarded its southern side as a military concern, but those reports have caused worry in Delhi.

What it means for the force: For decades, the corridor was seen as India's weak spot, a narrow neck someone could squeeze. This plan is designed to ensure it can withstand an attack and still function, keeping supplies flowing to the Northeast. If it becomes clear that the corridor can't be cut quickly, an adversary has less reason to try. The plan will be more effective if a single China facing theatre command is put in charge of the corridor, so that forces on both its northern and southern sides report to the same chain of command.

01

THREAT BOARD

From Musharraf's Guard to Pahalgam Suspect: Pakistan's Proxy War Gets a Paper Trail

The Army's Chinar Corps has confirmed that a Lashkar-e-Taiba terrorist was killed in Operation KORAG in the Palmaidan area of Budgam, near Yousmarg. Troops had been tracking him on an intelligence tip and came under fire. Security agencies identified him as Mohammad Asif, alias Hashim Moosa, one of the most wanted foreign terrorists in Jammu and Kashmir and a named suspect in the 2025 Pahalgam massacre, in which 26 tourists were killed. J&K Police had a Rs 20 lakh bounty on him.

According to security sources, Asif joined the Pakistan Army in 2000 and moved to the Special Services Group in 2005, serving with its 4 Commando "Yalgar" Battalion. Between 2006 and 2009 he was reportedly part of Pervez Musharraf's personal security detail. He retired as a havildar in 2023. A Pakistani identity card recovered by agencies reportedly helped confirm his record.

What the service record shows: For three decades, Rawalpindi has said the men crossing the LoC are freelancers it does not control. A soldier trusted to guard the country's military ruler, who turns up within two years of retirement as LeT's lead gunman in Kashmir, makes that harder to sustain. It also fits what investigators saw at Pahalgam. The attack was planned with the discipline of a trained unit, and the attackers stayed hidden in the forests for weeks. If the record holds up, India has documents to place before FATF and the UN. On the ground, LeT has lost a man with special forces training it will struggle to replace.

The Amritsar shooting: In Punjab, the method is cheaper. On a September evening, ASI Jaswant Singh of Amritsar police was shot while riding home. Amritsar Rural Police arrested five people within days. The two alleged shooters, Karanbir Singh Nandi and Gurpreet Singh alias Gopi, are from Jhanjoti village, and the other three are accused of sheltering them. Nandi fired on a police team near Jhander, was hit in the leg and chest, and later died. A constable was shot in the thigh, and another officer was saved by his bulletproof jacket. SSP Kanwalpreet Singh Chahal said the accused may have been in contact with a Pakistan-based handler. IG Gurpreet Singh Bhullar said foreign handlers had paid the two to carry out the attack.

Advertisement

The shooters were local men hired for cash. The handler stays in Pakistan, and if his men are caught or killed, he simply pays someone else.

Drugs, drones and money: Other recent cases suggest how this is funded and supplied. Off Lakshadweep, the Coast Guard stopped a dhow carrying 526 kg of heroin and methamphetamine, loaded at Gwadar and headed for a buyer in Punjab. Defence Ministry figures show 863 drone intrusions along the Pakistan border in 2025-26, nearly all over Punjab and Rajasthan. Of the drones shot down, 72 were carrying drugs and five carried weapons. Drug money keeps the network going, drones bring pistols and cash across, and handlers use that cash to recruit shooters. For attacks that need real training, such as in Kashmir, former Pakistani soldiers are sent in. As argued in a Firstpost piece this week, India needs to prepare for a drone war with Pakistan, and a small version of it already plays out on the Punjab border most nights. Low-flying drones carry a few kilos each, enough to arm a module like the one in Amritsar. BSF interceptions show India adapting, but detection along the entire border remains patchy.

After Operation Sindoor, Pakistan knows that a major attack traced back to it could prompt Indian missile strikes. Small, deniable attacks in Punjab and a few trained killers in Kashmir may seem a safer way to keep pressure on India below that threshold. But the Budgam case weakens the deniability that the approach depends on. Punjab Police broke the Amritsar module quickly, and the Army removed a Pahalgam suspect. The harder task is cutting off drug routes at sea and drone routes at the border before the money reaches a village in Majha.

Pakistan Fires Missile From Chinese-Built Submarine as India's Own Deal Waits

Pakistan's newly commissioned submarine PNS Hangor has test fired a missile, believed by defence sources to be China's YJ-18 anti ship cruise missile. The variant and its range are unconfirmed. Hangor is the first of eight submarines Pakistan is buying from China, four built in Chinese yards and four in Karachi. The test came less than two weeks after an incident at sea between an Indian warship and the Pakistani vessel PNS Hunain.

Advertisement

The undersea balance: A submarine that can stay hidden and fire anti-ship missiles is a real threat to any Indian fleet operating off Karachi, and eight of them is China arming Pakistan for a naval fight. India still holds the stronger hand. It has P-8I patrol aircraft, new shallow water submarine hunters like INS Malvan and a growing nuclear submarine fleet. The gap is conventional submarines. Project-75(I), meant to deliver six boats that can stay submerged for weeks, is still waiting for a contract after years of trials. Every Hangor that enters service makes that delay harder to justify.

AFSPA Extended in Parts of Manipur, Nagaland and Arunachal for Six Months

The Centre has extended AFSPA for six months from 1 October in specified areas of three northeastern states after reviewing the security situation. In Manipur, the whole state stays a "disturbed area" except the jurisdictions of 13 police stations in five valley districts. Nine districts of Nagaland are covered, along with parts of five others. In Arunachal, the Act stays in force in Tirap, Changlang and Longding and in three police station areas of Namsai.

On the ground: The map shows where Delhi still sees trouble. The Imphal valley police stations are out, while Manipur's hill districts stay in, where armed groups have operated since the 2023 violence. In Arunachal, Tirap, Changlang and Longding border Myanmar, where the civil war has pushed weapons and armed men across a porous frontier. Security forces have recovered large numbers of looted weapons in Manipur this year, and keeping AFSPA in place gives the Army and Assam Rifles the legal cover to keep up those search operations.

02

INDIA DEFENCE UPDATES

Army Seeks 1,547 Thermal Sights to Give Its Machine Guns Night Eyes

The Defence Ministry has issued a Request for Information for 1,547 thermal imaging night sights for the Army's 7.62 mm Medium Machine Guns. The requirement is that gunners can detect and engage a human target at 1,800 metres or more, by day or night. A thermal sight works by reading body heat rather than light, so it picks out a person in total darkness, through smoke and haze, and often behind light vegetation where the naked eye sees nothing.

Advertisement

What it means for the force: The MMG is the infantry's workhorse for sustained fire, the gun that holds a post, covers a gap in a fence or pins down an approaching party. Infiltration along the LoC almost always comes at night, and that has long given terrorists a window in which a defending post could hear movement but not hit it. A sight that matches the gun's full range closes that window. At 1,800 metres a gunner can spot and engage an infiltration group well before it reaches the wire. The order also fits a pattern. Earlier this year the Army cleared new day sights for its NEGEV light machine guns, with BEL leading production. Night-fighting optics for the infantry's basic weapons are being upgraded step by step, and India's growing thermal-imaging industry is well placed to supply them.

Army Helicopters Land on Highway Near Pakistan Border

The Army Aviation Corps landed and took off Rudra, Dhruv and Chetak helicopters on a stretch of NH-911 near Dantour in Rajasthan, close to the Pakistan border. The highway section was temporarily turned into a tactical landing zone to practise operating when airfields or helipads are damaged or out of reach. During Operation Sindoor, Pakistan aimed drones and missiles at Indian airbases. Fixed bases are the first targets in any fight. Helicopters that can land on any straight road near the front can refuel, rearm and keep flying even if a base is hit, and they become far harder to find. The IAF has done this with fighters on highway airstrips for years. The Army is now doing the same with its armed Rudras and utility helicopters in the western desert.

Army to Shield Key Installations With Layered Steel Mesh Against Drones

The Army wants three layer steel mesh screens to protect sensitive buildings in field areas from drones. Its Request for Information, asks for screens roughly 37 metres long and 20 metres wide. Each layer uses a different kind of mesh. The first slows a drone down, the second absorbs the impact and the third holds it. The first sets will go up in the western sector. Jammers and guns work until a swarm arrives or a drone flies in on a pre-set route that ignores jamming. A net needs no radar, no power and no operator. It sits over a command post or an ammunition store and catches what the other layers miss. Russian tanks in Ukraine went into battle with crude metal cages for the same reason. The Army has already fitted similar mesh over bunkers, guns and tanks, and is now scaling it up to whole buildings.

Advertisement

Para SF Trial Indian-Made G72 Submachine Gun

The Army's Para Special Forces are testing the G72, a 9 mm submachine gun built by Bengaluru's SSS Defence. It uses a roller delayed blowback action, which keeps the gun steady during automatic fire at around 900 rounds a minute. It has a folding stock, controls for left and right handed shooters and rails for sights, lights and lasers. The barrel takes a suppressor. Special forces clear rooms, ships and aircraft at close range, where a short, controllable gun matters more than range. Para SF units have mostly relied on imported submachine guns. If the G72 clears trials with India's toughest small arms users, police and paramilitary counter terror teams are likely to follow, and the spares and ammunition chain would stay in India.

03

PROCUREMENT AND INDUSTRY TRACKER

IdeaForge's ZOLT Drone Now Launches a Strike Drone in Mid-Air

Mumbai based ideaForge has shown its ZOLT tactical drone carrying and releasing an air launched effector, a smaller drone with a mission payload. After release, the effector steadies itself, switches to autonomous guided flight and heads for its target coordinates. ZOLT is already in service. The Army chose it after extensive field trials in electronic warfare environments, and it is designed for high threat, high altitude and signal contested environments, with the ability to operate without GPS and resist communication jamming. The company had flagged progress on air launched effects and fuel hybrid long endurance capability for ZOLT earlier this financial year.

Why it matters: This splits one mission across two machines. The larger, more expensive carrier stays back, outside the reach of enemy air defence, while the cheap effector goes forward and takes the risk. That stretches the strike range of a tactical drone without sending the valuable airframe into danger. It is the same mothership logic behind the large loyal wingman programmes abroad, scaled down for a battalion commander instead of a fighter pilot. For the Army, which is raising dedicated drone units and pushing drones down to its armoured and artillery formations, this is the kind of layered unmanned strike that worked in Ukraine. It is still a demonstration. Whether it turns into an order will depend on Army trials, but an Indian firm is now building the concept in-house, on a platform already proven against jamming.

Advertisement

GE to Deliver Four More F404 Engines by December as Tejas Mk-2 Gets a Flight Window

Defence Secretary Rajesh Kumar Singh has confirmed that GE will deliver four F404 engines for the Tejas Mk-1A between October and December 2026. Engine shortages have been the main reason HAL's Mk-1A production has lagged. He also gave a timeline for the next jets. The Tejas Mk-2, a heavier, longer range successor powered by the more powerful GE F414 and carrying the indigenous Uttam AESA radar, is targeted to fly between June and September 2027. The AMCA prototype is targeted for September 2028.

Bottom line: Four engines will not clear HAL's backlog. They do show the supply line is moving again, and the IAF needs every Tejas it can get as MiG-21s retire and its squadron count stays well short of the sanctioned 42. The larger point is the dependence underneath. India's entire light fighter line has waited on one American supplier's factory schedule, and Mk-2 will rely on the same company's F414. The firm dates for Mk-2 and AMCA give India a clear deadline for the Kaveri revival and its other engine partnerships to deliver. Until India makes its own fighter engine, how many jets roll out of Bengaluru will be decided partly in the United States.

Paras Defence to Build Optics for DRDO's Space-Based Hyperspectral Payload

Paras Defence has won a Rs 26.59 crore DRDO order to design and build the optics and opto-mechanical unit for a hyperspectral payload that will fly in space. The company is the lead integrator and has until September 2027 to deliver. A hyperspectral sensor breaks light into hundreds of narrow bands. Each material reflects those bands in its own pattern, so the sensor can tell paint from metal and fresh soil from old ground.

What it adds: That is the property that defeats camouflage. A net over a vehicle may look like grass to a normal camera, but it won't reflect light the way grass does. From orbit, a hyperspectral sensor can flag hidden vehicles, new digging and dummy equipment, which matters along a LAC where China keeps building. ISRO flew one such satellite, HySIS, in 2018. This order puts a private Indian company in charge of the hardest part of the next payload, the optics.

Advertisement

DRDO Targets Two Import Gaps: Armoured Vehicle Glass and Fighter Radios

DRDO is working with CSIR's Central Glass and Ceramic Research Institute in Kolkata on a Rs 50 crore project to make bulletproof glass for armoured vehicles in India. The glass is 30 to 50 percent lighter than the imported glass now in use and has already stopped rounds from the Trichy Assault Rifle, India's version of the AK-47, in early trials. Separately, DRDO expects to

finish a software defined radio for the IAF by the end of this year, after delivering Army and Navy versions that BEL is now producing. Because the radio runs on software, the same set can switch frequencies, change encryption or join a different network with a new program.

What it means for the force: Lighter glass lets armoured vehicles carry more armour or load and handle better on hill roads, which matters most to troops on patrol in J&K and the Northeast. The radio carries more weight. IAF fighters currently talk over B-Net, an Israeli system bought in 2017, and whoever writes a radio's code controls its encryption and updates. An Indian radio means India can patch it quickly if an enemy learns to jam it, and a common radio across all three services would let a pilot speak directly to troops on the ground, something the planned theatre commands will need.

Tonbo Builds Made-in-India Targeting Turret for Large Drones

Bengaluru based Tonbo Imaging has built the Avenger S75E, a stabilised camera turret for large drones, helicopters and aircraft. It combines a daylight camera with short wave and mid wave infrared sensors behind a single lens, plus a laser rangefinder and designator. It weighs under 55 kg. An onboard processor runs AI software that picks out targets and keeps tracking them on its own.

What it adds: A large surveillance drone is only as good as the sensor ball under its nose. Indian Herons and MQ-9Bs fly with foreign ones. Short wave infrared cuts through haze and smoke, and mid-wave infrared spots body and engine heat at night. The laser designator lets a drone mark a target for a guided bomb dropped by another aircraft. An Indian made turret could go on Indian drones such as the armed Archer-NG and the Coast Guard's planned long-endurance fleet. No order has been announced yet.

Advertisement

Kaveri Engine Clears Russian Trials, Heads for Ghatak Stealth Drone

DRDO's Kaveri derivative engine has reportedly completed high altitude and in flight trials in Russia, flown on an Il-76 test aircraft. It produced 48.5 kN of thrust, above the 46 kN target. This version drops the afterburner, which saves fuel and suits a long-range drone. It is meant to power Ghatak, India's planned stealth flying-wing combat drone. Indian certification and integration are still pending, and induction is estimated two to three years away.

Why Ghatak needs it: Kaveri was dropped from Tejas because it fell short on thrust. It has now found a job it can actually do. A stealth drone built to slip into enemy airspace and hit radars and command posts needs an engine India controls fully, since no foreign supplier will easily power that kind of weapon. Success here would also give DRDO a tested engine core to build on for bigger programmes.

04

EXERCISES, DIPLOMACY AND PARTNERSHIPS

French Air Force Studies Operation Sindoor as a Benchmark for Modern Air War

France's Air and Space Force is studying how the IAF fought Operation Sindoor. Its Vice Chief, Lt Gen Dominique Tardif, said the number of aircraft operating at the same time in one contested battlespace had no parallel since perhaps World War II. Speaking in Jodhpur during the second edition of the IAF's multinational exercise Tarang Shakti, he said France has already held talks with the IAF on the lessons, though India is sharing only what it considers safe, since much of the operation remains sensitive. He added that drawing real conclusions will take time, because analysts need the records from every system involved.

Reading between the lines: Western air forces have trained for decades for large, layered air campaigns, but none has fought one recently against a modern air force with AEW&C, long-range missiles and dense air defences on the other side. That makes India the case study, a reversal of the usual flow of doctrine from West to East. France has a specific stake. It is weighing longer-range air-to-air missiles for its Rafales, because the Meteor both air forces carry reaches about 150 km while some Chinese, Russian and American missiles reportedly go past 300 km. Sindoor was fought largely beyond visual range, so how far shots were taken and how they landed is precious data. India controls who sees it. And the air force that knows the Rafale best is studying the IAF's performance, which says more about Pakistan's shoot-down claims than any rebuttal could.

Advertisement

Indian-Designed Kaalbhairav and YAMA Drones to Be Built in Portugal

Bengaluru-based Flying Wedge Defence & Aerospace (FWDA) will manufacture two of its drones in Portugal through a tie up with Keydef, the defence arm of Portuguese tech firm Sketchpixel. Kaalbhairav Lite is a 50 kg autonomous aircraft that can fly for five to 15 hours carrying up to 10 kg of sensors or munitions, used for surveillance or precision strike depending on the payload. YAMA is an interceptor drone built to hunt hostile drones, including swarms. Keydef is putting about Rs 65 crore into FWDA's technology and will add electronics and AI work, and both firms plan to pursue NATO certification for the Portuguese built systems.

The bigger picture: Indian defence exports have so far meant shipping finished products abroad. Here European money is buying into Indian intellectual property and building it on European soil, while the design stays Indian. The timing works in India's favour. Europe is rearming after Ukraine, drones and counter drone systems top the shopping list, and European procurement increasingly favours kit made inside the bloc. A Portuguese production line could give an Indian design that access, along with a NATO stamp if certification comes through. YAMA is the sharper bet. Cheap interceptors that kill drones without spending a costly missile are what every European army is short of, and Indian firms have been building them against a live threat on the western border since Operation Sindoor.

INS Ranvijay Exercises With Omani Navy Off Salalah

Destroyer INS Ranvijay called at Salalah in Oman and carried out a passage exercise with the Omani patrol vessel RNOV Sadh. Oman lets Indian warships use its port at Duqm, a rare arrangement for India in the Gulf. Salalah lies on the route to the Gulf of Aden, where the Navy has run anti piracy patrols since 2008. Gwadar, the Pakistani port China runs, is a short sail to the north-east. Port calls like this one keep Indian ships familiar with Omani waters and keep Muscat close at a time when Pakistan and China are active on the other side of the Arabian Sea.

Advertisement

India and South Korea Revive Stalled K30 Biho Air Defence Deal

India and South Korea have reopened talks on the K30 Biho, a Hanwha-built tracked air defence vehicle that the Army chose years ago and never bought. The subject came up at the 10th India-Korea Joint Committee meeting on defence industries and logistics in New Delhi. Biho pairs twin 30 mm cannons with short-range missiles on one chassis and drives alongside tanks, shooting down drones, helicopters and low-flying cruise missiles. It reportedly beat Russia's Tunguska-M1 and Pantsir in Indian trials, and the DAC cleared it in 2021. The deal then stalled over how much would be built in India. The requirement is around 104 systems. No fresh approval or timeline has been announced.

What's at stake: India's air defence did well in Operation Sindoor, but most of it was guarding fixed targets like airbases and cities. A strike corps pushing into the Rajasthan or Punjab plains leaves that umbrella behind, and today it would move under ageing Shilka and Tunguska guns. Biho is built for that gap. The cannons do most of the work against cheap drones, so a Rs 10 lakh Turkish made drone isn't met with a missile worth many times more. Korea has also shown it will actually build in India. The K9 Vajra howitzers rolling out of L&T's Hazira plant came from the same partnership, and both sides agreed at this meeting to revive their 2020 defence industry roadmap. For Delhi, Seoul is a supplier that carries neither the sanctions risk of Russian kit nor the export politics that come with American systems. The sticking point remains the same one that killed the deal last time: how much Hanwha will hand over.

India and Kazakhstan Begin Counter-Terror Exercise KAZIND-2026

The ninth edition of the India-Kazakhstan military exercise KAZIND opened in Oskemen in eastern Kazakhstan and runs till 11 October. India has sent 60 personnel, mostly from the Garhwal Rifles along with IAF members. Troops will train for UN-mandated counter terror operations in mountains and small towns, covering heliborne raids, cordon and search, and the use of drones and counter drone systems.

209.title: Assam Rifles conducts civic action, welfare drives across Na
209.description: Assam Rifles conducts cleanliness drives, plantation activities, and community welfare events across Nagaland.
209.text:
An Assam Rifles personnel assists a student and a resident in watering a newly planted sapling in Nagaland on October 2.





DIMAPUR — Assam Rifles conducted multiple civic action programmes, including mass cleanliness campaigns, plantation drives, and educational and welfare initiatives across various locations in Nagaland on October 2.





In Kohima, Assam Rifles organised a mass cleanliness drive to mark Gandhi Jayanti on the theme “Swachhata Hi Seva – Ek Din, Ek Ghanta, Ek Saath”.





The campaign witnessed participation from various sections of society, including representatives from D Block Youth Organisation, Zub Zub NGO, Kohima Municipal Council, Assam Rifles Ex-Servicemen Association Kohima, Kendriya Vidyalaya, Mount Olive College, Chandmari Higher Secondary School, Little Flower Higher Secondary School, National Cadet Corps cadets, Border Security Force, Central Reserve Police Force, and Assam Rifles personnel.





The programme commenced with a ceremony at Children's Park, Kohima Garrison, where Thenusou Sekhose, Deputy Chairperson of Kohima Municipal Council, along with officials of Assam Rifles, paid floral tributes to Mahatma Gandhi. The cleanliness drive proceeded from Children's Park through Phulbari Chowk to Razhu Point before returning to the starting point.





Read more local news: North Eastern Council seeks ambitious projects from Nagaland



Inter-school math quiz for private schools held in Dimapur





In Kohima, Assam Rifles also visited Bright Morning Star Children Home, where personnel distributed gifts and essential commodities to the children and staff.

210.title: Yogasana Can Become Major International Sport, Says Manipur CM Khemchand
210.description: Manipur CM Yumnam Khemchand Singh says Yogasana can emerge as a major international sport and urges athletes to prepare for global competitions.
210.text:
Ads

Manipur Chief Minister Yumnam Khemchand Singh said Yogasana has the potential to emerge as a major international sporting discipline. He urged Indian athletes to prepare themselves for competitions at the highest global level.

The chief minister made the remarks while inaugurating the 38th National Yogasana Championship 2026 at Khuman Lampak Main Indoor Stadium in Imphal.

He said Yogasana, rooted in India’s ancient traditions, had gained a global presence. He also expressed hope that the discipline could eventually become part of the Olympic Games.

The championship will continue from October 2 to 4. It also serves as a selection trial for India’s team for the 12th World Yogasana Championship, scheduled to take place in Thailand in 2027.

Read More: BR Patil Seeks Rahul Gandhi’s Intervention on Karnataka Land Reforms Act

Khemchand Urges Athletes to Prepare for Global Competitions

Addressing athletes and officials, Khemchand called for systematic preparation and sustained efforts to achieve success at international competitions.

He said Indian Yogasana players should prepare themselves both mentally and physically. He encouraged them to aim for strong performances at world championships and other international events.

The chief minister also drew a comparison with hockey. He said India’s long association with the sport had not always translated into consistent success at the highest level.

Through this example, he highlighted the importance of regular training and long-term preparation.

Khemchand said athletes must begin preparing for the global sporting stage now if they want to achieve success in the future.

National Yogasana Championship Begins in Imphal

The 38th National Yogasana Championship is being organised by the Manipur Yoga Society in collaboration with the All-India Yoga Culture Federation.

The event brings together participants from different states across India.

Alongside the championship, organisers are conducting selection trials for the Indian team for the 12th World Yogasana Championship 2027 in Thailand.

The event carries the theme “Yogasana for Health, Harmony and National Unity.”

The championship aims to provide athletes with a platform to demonstrate their skills and compete at the national level.

CM Highlights Yoga’s Global Recognition

Khemchand recalled the growing international recognition of Yoga following the United Nations General Assembly’s adoption of the International Day of Yoga in 2014.

He referred to the initiative that led to the observance of June 21 as International Yoga Day.

The chief minister also spoke about his association with Yoga since 2014. He said he had participated in efforts to promote the practice at the grassroots level.

He recalled programmes that created awareness about Yoga and its benefits for the body and mind.

Khemchand stressed that Yoga should not be viewed merely as physical exercise. He described it as a practice that supports overall well-being.

Sanskrit and India’s Ancient Knowledge Traditions

The chief minister also spoke about India’s ancient knowledge traditions, including Sanskrit.

He said the classical language had attracted interest beyond India, including in academic and technological circles in Europe.

Khemchand referred to Sanskrit’s structure and vocabulary while discussing its relevance in modern academic and technological contexts.

He connected this discussion with the wider international interest in India’s traditional knowledge systems.

Athletes Asked to Carry Message of Peace from Manipur

Welcoming participants from different states, Khemchand urged them to carry a message of peace from Manipur when they return home.

He appealed to the athletes to share a positive message about the state and its people.

The chief minister also interacted with participants and wished them success in the championship and selection trials.

Manipur’s Home and Youth Affairs and Sports Minister Govindas Konthoujam also attended the opening ceremony.

He spoke about Yoga’s role in promoting physical fitness, discipline, concentration, mental balance and perseverance.

Yogasana’s International Sporting Aspirations

The championship comes amid efforts to expand Yogasana’s presence as a competitive sport.

The upcoming World Yogasana Championship in Thailand will provide another international platform for athletes.

Khemchand’s remarks placed emphasis on preparation, international exposure and the long-term development of the discipline.

He called on Indian athletes to work towards competing at the highest level, including the possibility of future Olympic participation.

Yogasana is not currently an Olympic sport. Its potential inclusion in major international sporting events remains a future aspiration.

The three-day national championship in Imphal will continue until October 4, with athletes also competing for places in India’s team for the 2027 world championship.

Read More: BR Patil Seeks Rahul Gandhi’s Intervention on Karnataka Land Reforms Act

211.title: Indian Army’s Spear Corps, APS Agartala students hold Swachhata Hi Seva drive
211.description: Spear Corps and APS Agartala students joined Swachhata Hi Seva activities in Agartala, ending with a cleanliness drive at Albert Ekka War Memorial.
211.text:
Troops of the Indian Army’s Spear Corps, in collaboration with students of Army Public School (APS) Agartala, organised a multi-day series of educational and community outreach activities from September 29 to October 2 at the Agartala Military Station as part of the nationwide ‘Swachhata Hi Seva’ campaign.

The initiative aimed to promote environmental awareness, personal hygiene, and civic responsibility among both students and military personnel. The four-day campaign concluded on October 2 with a large-scale cleanliness drive at the Albert Ekka War Memorial, honouring the nation’s fallen heroes through community service. At the same time, Spear Corps volunteers conducted a station-wide Shramdaan, or voluntary cleanliness drive, across the garrison.

ADVERTISEMENT

Stay connected Make The News Mill your preferred source See more TNM stories when you search for news on Google. Add TNM on Google

To encourage sustainable habits among young participants, APS Agartala hosted various competitions across multiple grade levels. These included banner and poster-making contests focusing on the Swachh Bharat Campaign, an essay writing competition on public health and hygiene solutions, and a drawing contest themed ‘Clean, Green & Sustainable Station’, where students presented ideas for environmentally friendly military stations.

Meanwhile, Army personnel undertook an extensive cleanliness drive within the cantonment, clearing waste, maintaining green belts, enhancing public transit corridors, and promoting eco-friendly waste disposal methods throughout residential and operational areas.

ADVERTISEMENT

A defence spokesperson stated, “Inculcating environmental responsibility and civic pride in our youth is as vital as maintaining operational readiness. The active involvement of our students at APS Agartala alongside the dedicated Shramdaan by our troops reflects the true spirit of Swachhata Hi Seva—turning civic duty into a shared, lifelong commitment.”

The Spear Corps, tasked with defending India’s borders and ensuring security in the North-East, regularly leads initiatives related to ecological preservation, humanitarian relief, and civic welfare alongside its core operational duties.

212.title: Spear Corps, APS students join Swachhata Hi Seva drive in Agartala
212.description: Indian Army’s Spear Corps, APS students observe 'Swachhata Hi Seva' drive at Agartala Military Station
212.text:
Agartala (Tripura) [India], October 3 (ANI): In line with the nationwide 'Swachhata Hi Seva' campaign, troops of the Indian Army’s Spear Corps, in collaboration with students of Army Public School (APS) Agartala, organised a multi-day series of educational, creative, and community outreach drives from September 29 to October 2 at the Agartala Military Station.

The campaign aimed to instil deep environmental consciousness, personal hygiene, and active civic responsibility among young students and military personnel alike.

The four-day initiative culminated on October 2 with a massive outdoor cleanliness drive at the iconic Albert Ekka War Memorial, paying tribute to the nation's fallen heroes through community service, alongside a station-wide Shramdaan (voluntary cleanliness drive) undertaken by Spear Corps volunteers across the garrison.

To foster sustainable habits from an early age, APS Agartala conducted a series of competitions across various grade levels. These included banner- and poster-making activities focused on the 'Swachh Bharat Campaign', an essay writing competition on public health and hygiene solutions, and a drawing contest themed 'Clean, Green & Sustainable Station', where students showcased creative blueprints for eco-friendly military stations.

Simultaneously, Army personnel participated in an extensive cleanliness drive across the cantonment. Troops cleared waste, maintained green belts, beautified public transit corridors, and promoted eco-friendly waste disposal mechanisms throughout the station's residential and operational lines.

"Inculcating environmental responsibility and civic pride in our youth is as vital as maintaining operational readiness. The active involvement of our students at APS Agartala alongside the dedicated Shramdaan by our troops reflects the true spirit of Swachhata Hi Seva—turning civic duty into a shared, lifelong commitment," said a defence spokesperson.

The Spear Corps of the Indian Army, tasked with defending India's borders and maintaining security in the North-East, routinely spearheads ecological preservation, humanitarian relief, and civic welfare initiatives alongside its core operational responsibilities.

(ANI)

213.title: Indian Army completes tourist rescue Operation Him Setu in North Sikkim landslide
213.text:
The evacuation of all tourists stranded due to a landslide between Lachen and Chungthang in North Sikkim was successfully completed today under the Operation Him Setu launched by the Indian Army’s Trishakti Corps.

Special buses and vehicles were arranged to transport tourists from Taram Chu via Chungthang to Gangtok.

After the operation, Minister of Social Welfare Mr Samdup Lepcha met officials of the Army and the Border Roads Organisation and expressed his gratitude for their continuous efforts. Mr Lepcha said that despite adverse weather and logistical challenges, the mission was successfully accomplished through collective effort and community spirit.
